Passage – 3


The determination of criminal liability of children under Indian law requires a layered analysis under the Juvenile Justice (Care and
Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act), read with principles of criminal law under the Indian Penal Code (IPC). While a "child" is any
person below 18 years, the law differentiates between categories of children based on age, nature of offence, and degree of mental
culpability.


Offences are classified into petty, serious, and heinous, with heinous offences being those carrying a minimum punishment of seven years
or more. In cases involving children aged 16-18 years accused of heinous offences, the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) must conduct a
preliminary assessment into (i) mental and physical capacity to commit the offence, (ii) ability to understand consequences, and (iii)
circumstances of commission.
This assessment is not a trial but a jurisdictional filter, determining whether the child should be subjected to adult criminal process.
Such transfer is exceptional, not routine. The law does not equate chronological age with adult culpability, nor does it permit substitution
of statutory criteria with societal perceptions of gravity or outrage. Failure to apply the correct parameters vitiates the transfer decision.


Parallelly, under the IPC, the doctrine of doli incapax introduces a graduated immunity: children below 7 are absolutely exempt, while those
between 7 and 12 are exempt only if they lack sufficient maturity to understand the nature and consequences of their act. This doctrine
concerns capacity to commit an offence, whereas the JJ Act concerns forum and manner of trial, though both may intersect.


Even where a child is tried as an adult, the JJ framework continues to influence sentencing architecture, ensuring that punishment is not
purely retributive. Thus, the inquiry is not binary but involves distinguishing between capacity, classification, procedural compliance, and
residual protection.

following is the most accurate legal position regarding the validity of the JJB's decision?
options: Valid, as brutality reflects sufficient understanding of consequences.
Valid, as heinous offences justify adult trial irrespective of assessment depth.
Invalid, because statutory factors cannot be substituted with societal considerations.
Invalid only if A proves lack of maturity.

Section 4 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs the communication of proposals (offers), acceptances, and revocations, and
determines the exact moment at which each becomes complete. The provision introduces a deliberate asymmetry between the position
of the proposer and the acceptor.


The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Thus, mere dispatch of

an offer is insufficient; knowledge is essential.


However, communication of acceptance operates differently. As against the proposer, communication of acceptance is complete when it
is put into a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor. As against the acceptor, it is complete when it
comes to the knowledge of the proposer.


This creates a dual-timing rule: the proposer becomes bound earlier (on dispatch), while the acceptor becomes bound later (on receipt).


Revocation follows a similar dual structure. A proposal may be revoked at any time before communication of its acceptance is complete
as against the proposer, but not afterwards. Likewise, an acceptance may be revoked at any time before communication of acceptance is
complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards.
Thus, an acceptance may be revoked even after it has been dispatched, provided the revocation reaches the proposer before the
acceptance itself comes to his knowledge.


The scheme of Section 4 therefore hinges on identifying:
(i) when knowledge is acquired,
(ii) when transmission becomes irreversible, and
(iii) the relative timing of acceptance and revocation.


In cases of instantaneous modes of communication, such as telephone, telex, or email, the rule differs. Communication of acceptance is
complete only when it is received by the proposer, as such modes do not involve any time lag between transmission and receipt.
Therefore, in such cases, the acceptor is bound only when the acceptance comes to the knowledge of the proposer, and the proposer
becomes bound at the same moment.


Further, acceptance must ordinarily be made in the same manner as the proposal is communicated, unless the proposer prescribes a
different mode or waives such requirement.

acceptance complete as against A?
options: 2 PM (when letter was posted)
3 PM (when email was sent)
3 PM (when email was received by A)
1 PM (when offer was read by B)

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required to
choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 5


Defamation consists in making or publishing any imputation concerning a person, by words spoken or written, or by visible representation,
with the intention, knowledge, or reason to believe that such imputation will harm the reputation of that person. Reputation refers to the
estimation of a person in the eyes of others, and not merely the opinion of the person defamed about himself.


An imputation may be express or implied. Even a statement framed as an opinion may amount to defamation if it conveys or is
understood to convey underlying assertions of fact which are not disclosed, thereby lowering the person's reputation.


Publication is complete when the imputation is communicated to any person other than the person to whom it relates. Such
communication need not be intentional; it is sufficient if the imputation is in fact conveyed to a third party, even through unintended or
indirect means.


The mental element does not require a specific intention to harm; it is sufficient if the maker knew or had reason to believe that the
imputation would harm reputation. Absence of malice does not by itself exclude liability.


Truth may operate as a defence only where the imputation is shown to be both true and made for the public good. Truth alone, without

public purpose, is insufficient.


Thus, determination of defamation involves assessing:
(i) whether the statement contains an imputation (express or implied),
(ii) whether it was published,
(iii) whether the requisite mental element exists, and
(iv) whether any exception applies.

options: Not defamation, because the statement is merely an opinion
Defamation, because the statement implies undisclosed defamatory facts
Not defamation, because no specific allegation is made
Defamation only if A intended to harm B

On a lazy Sunday afternoon, the children of Sunflower Apartments gathered in the courtyard, looking for a way to make their weekend
more exciting. Inspired by their love for mystery stories and treasure hunts, they decided to invent a secret address game. Instead of using
regular flat or floor numbers, they began writing coded notes to one another using creative symbols and clues.


The game quickly caught on, and soon every message became a puzzle to decode. There are ten residents in the building, identified by the
initials A to J. The building has five floors and ten flats, with five flats on the left wing and five on the right wing. None of the flats are
vacant, and no two residents live in the same flat.


To make the game more challenging, the children designed a unique coding system to represent each resident's address. The codes they
used are as follows:


Xn$Y means X lives n floors above Y (on the same wing)
Xn#Y means X lives n floors below Y (on the same wing)
X&Y means X is immediately to the left of Y (on the same floor)
X@Y means X is immediately to the right of Y (on the same floor)


Some of the coded notes written by the children are as follows:


F@C2$A ; E&B3$D ; G@A3#H ; D2#J@H

Directions for questions 83 to 108: Read the passages and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 3


On the afternoon of March 14th, a rare first-edition copy of "The Forgotten Compass" - valued at Rs. 4,80,000 and owned by collector
Devraj Sinha - went missing from Stall No. 7 at the Horizon International Book Fair. The fair operates daily from 10:00 AM to 8:00 PM, and
all stall-holders are required to vacate the premises by 8:30 PM. Security cameras cover all four entry and exit gates but do not cover the
interior of individual stalls.


The book was confirmed present by Devraj himself at 3:15 PM, when he left his stall briefly to attend a panel discussion in Hall B, which
ran from 3:20 PM to 5:00 PM. His stall assistant, Meena, was supposed to manage the stall in his absence but left the stall unattended at
3:45 PM for approximately 25 minutes to use the restroom facility located at the far end of the fairground. Devraj returned to the stall at
5:05 PM and discovered the book missing.


Three individuals were identified as persons of interest:
• Farhan, a rival book dealer, was seen by a vendor in the adjacent Stall No. 6 browsing Stall No. 7 between 3:50 PM and 4:10 PM. Farhan
claims he was merely admiring the display and left without touching anything. He was spotted at Gate 2 by a security camera at 4:25 PM,
which is a 12-minute walk from Stall No. 7.
• Geeta, a known rare-book enthusiast, had her entry badge scanned at Gate 1 at 3:30 PM and was seen at the food court - located
adjacent to Hall B - at 4:55 PM by two independent fair volunteers. The food court is a 5-minute walk from Stall No. 7.
• Harish, the stall's part-time helper, had worked the morning shift (10:00 AM to 2:00 PM) and officially clocked out at 2:05 PM. His exit was
recorded by the Gate 3 camera. However, a vendor at a nearby stall claims to have seen someone matching Harish's description near Stall
No. 7 around 4:30 PM.
• The fair's inventory log, which all stall-holders must update after each transaction or notable event, shows no entry made by Meena
during her solo supervision period from 3:15 PM to 5:05 PM.
content.questionText:
[Establishing the Precise Theft Window]
Based strictly on the information provided, what is the narrowest time window within which the theft must have occurred?
options:
Between 3:15 PM and 5:05 PM, because the book was confirmed present when Devraj left and discovered missing when he returned,
making this the outer boundary of the theft window.

Between 3:45 PM and 4:10 PM, because the stall was unattended only during Meena's absence and Farhan was the only identified
person known to have been inside the stall during that period.

Between 3:45 PM and 5:00 PM, because the stall became unattended at 3:45 PM and Devraj was in the panel discussion until 5:00 PM,
meaning no authorised person was present to observe the theft.

Between 3:50 PM and 4:10 PM, because only Farhan was placed inside Stall No. 7 by a witness, and this is the only period corroborated
by direct observation of an unidentified person at the scene.

[Evaluating Sufficiency of an Alibi]
Geeta's alibi places her at the food court at 4:55 PM. Can this single fact conclusively rule her out as the suspect, and why?
options:
Yes, because 4:55 PM is after the theft window closes at 4:10 PM, and being placed at the food court confirms she was not near the stall
at the only time the theft could have occurred during Farhan's visit.

No, because even though she was at the food court at 4:55 PM, there is no confirmed account of her movements between 3:30 PM and
4:55 PM - a gap of 85 minutes - during which she could have visited Stall No. 7 and still reached the food court in time.

Yes, because Gate 1 is at the opposite end of the fairground from Stall No. 7, which means her entry location makes it physically
impossible to have reached the stall within the relevant theft window of 3:45 PM to 4:10 PM.

No, because her status as a rare-book enthusiast creates a strong motive, and in legal reasoning, motive combined with opportunity is
sufficient to establish guilt beyond the level required to rule out a suspect entirely.

[Identifying a Logical Contradiction in Witness Evidence]
The vendor's claim that someone matching Harish's description was near Stall No. 7 at 4:30 PM directly conflicts with which established
piece of evidence, and what is the legal significance of this conflict?
options:
It conflicts with the Gate 3 camera record showing Harish's exit at 2:05 PM; the legal significance is that one of these two accounts must
be false or erroneous, which weakens Harish's confirmed exit as a definitive alibi and warrants further investigation.

It conflicts with Devraj's confirmation that the book was present at 3:15 PM; the legal significance is that Harish could have been near the
stall even before Devraj left, which expands the window in which Harish may have planned the theft.

It conflicts with Meena's 25-minute absence period; the legal significance is that because Meena and the vendor both observed events
simultaneously, only one of their accounts can be treated as reliable, and the vendor's account takes precedence as a neutral third party.

It conflicts with Farhan's confirmed sighting between 3:50 PM and 4:10 PM; the legal significance is that two unrelated persons cannot
occupy the same stall simultaneously, so if Farhan was present, Harish cannot have been, which exonerates Harish entirely.

[Applying the Principle of Inference from Omission]
The inventory log shows no entry made by Meena during her supervision period (3:15 PM to 5:05 PM). What is the most legally
significant inference that can be drawn from this omission, and what are its limits?
options:
It conclusively proves that Meena was complicit in the theft because she had a duty to log notable events and her failure to record the
theft constitutes an attempt to conceal the crime from the fair's records.

It suggests that either no notable event occurred during her supervision or that she failed in her duty to log one; however, it cannot
establish guilt because an omission in a log proves neither the theft's occurrence nor Meena's knowledge of or involvement in it.

It is irrelevant to the investigation because inventory logs are administrative documents not designed to capture criminal activity, and
their absence cannot be treated as evidence of either guilt or negligence in a legal context.

It establishes that the theft occurred after Meena returned at 4:10 PM, because if the theft had happened during her absence, she would
have noted the missing book upon her return and made a log entry at that point.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 83 to 108: Read the passages and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 4


The prospect of communicating with extraterrestrial intelligence has fascinated both scientists and writers, yet the frameworks guiding
this pursuit often reflect human assumptions more than objective possibility. Early speculative works imagined alien communication as
fundamentally different from human language, involving unfamiliar sensory modes or non-linear structures. In contrast, modern scientific
approaches tend to rely on models that resemble human cognition, implicitly assuming that alien beings would think and communicate in
comparable ways.


Such anthropocentric thinking imposes significant limitations. Efforts to detect extraterrestrial signals frequently depend on technologies
like radio transmission, presuming that alien civilizations would develop similar tools and use them in recognisable ways. This not only
narrows the search but also defines "communication" in strictly human terms, potentially excluding forms that do not align with our
expectations.


The continued absence of empirical evidence reinforces these concerns. Despite decades of systematic efforts, no confirmed
extraterrestrial signals have been identified. This silence challenges the assumption that intelligent life is both common and detectable.
Evolutionary theory further suggests that the emergence of human-like intelligence is shaped by highly specific conditions, making its
replication elsewhere uncertain rather than inevitable.


Even if extraterrestrial intelligence exists, meaningful communication may remain elusive. Some theories propose that mathematics or
logic could serve as universal languages, but these rely on the assumption that all intelligent beings perceive and structure reality similarly.
However, differences in perception or cognition could produce entirely distinct systems of meaning. Human difficulties in interpreting
animal communication or ancient symbolic scripts demonstrate how challenging understanding can be, even within familiar contexts.


Given these uncertainties, a more flexible approach may be necessary. Rather than projecting human models onto unknown forms of life,
the study of alien communication might benefit from considering radically different possibilities. In doing so, it not only broadens the
search for extraterrestrial contact but also deepens our understanding of the nature and limits of language itself.
content.questionText: The author's critique of current extraterrestrial communication methods is based on which underlying assumption?
options: alien civilizations are more advanced than humans
human methods of communication are universally applicable
alien intelligence may not resemble human cognition
extraterrestrial life does not exist

Natural gas trade plays a crucial role in the global energy market, linking major exporters with energy-deficient nations. Countries like
Russia, Qatar, and Iran are among the largest exporters, supplying liquefied natural gas (LNG) to various countries around the world.
Importing countries, including Japan, India, Brazil and Germany, depend heavily on these supplies to meet their industrial and domestic
energy needs. The dynamics of natural gas trade are influenced by geopolitical factors, infrastructure like pipelines and LNG terminals, and
fluctuating prices. As the world transitions toward cleaner energy sources, natural gas continues to serve as an important bridge fuel in
the global energy mix.


Three countries - Russia, Qatar, and Iran - export natural gas to four importing countries - India, Japan, Germany, and Brazil. All quantities
are measured in million cubic meters (MCM).


During a particular year, Russia exported 480 MCM, Qatar exported 420 MCM, and Iran exported 600 MCM. It is also known that 40% of

Russia's exports went to India, and the remaining exports were distributed among Japan, Germany, and Brazil in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Qatar
exported equal quantities to India and Japan, and the remaining exports were sent to Germany and Brazil in the ratio 2 : 3. Iran exported
30% of its gas to Germany and 25% to Japan. The remaining exports were divided between India and Brazil such that India received twice
as much as Brazil. The ratio of Germany's imports from Russia to its imports from Qatar is 8 : 7.
content.questionText: How much natural gas (in MCM) did India receive in total from all three exporting countries?

Prime Mock CLAT - 9 2027
Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


The British Empire’s policy of indirect rule in colonial India represented a sophisticated form of administrative control that has been both
praised for its efficiency and criticized for its divisive consequences. Unlike direct rule, which involved wholesale replacement of
indigenous institutions with British administrative structures, indirect rule sought to govern through existing native hierarchies and
traditional authorities. This approach was not merely pragmatic-born out of the vastness of the subcontinent and the limited number of
British administrators-but also reflected a calculated strategy to minimize resistance while maximizing control.


The system operated through a complex web of relationships between British officials and Indian princes, zamindars, and other traditional
power holders. The British Resident, typically stationed at princely courts, wielded considerable influence while maintaining the fiction of
native sovereignty. This arrangement allowed the British to claim legitimacy through traditional sources of authority while ensuring that
real power remained in colonial hands. The princes retained ceremonial functions and limited administrative control over internal affairs,
but foreign policy, defense, and ultimately all significant decisions rested with the British.


However, this policy had profound and lasting consequences for Indian society. By preserving and often ossifying traditional hierarchies,
indirect rule reinforced caste distinctions and communal divisions that might otherwise have evolved or diminished. The British found it
convenient to categorize Indians along religious and caste lines, creating administrative categories that became politically significant. This
taxonomic approach to governance contributed to the crystallization of identities that would later manifest in communal tensions and
ultimately influence the partition of 1947. The policy also created a class of collaborating elites who became dependent on British
patronage, complicating the nationalist movement’s efforts to present a unified front against colonial rule.


(390 words | Adapted from: Cambridge Companion to British Imperial History)

options: Emphasize the complete powerlessness of Indian rulers under British control.
Highlight the deliberate deception inherent in the colonial administrative strategy.
Suggest that native sovereignty was a legal technicality without practical significance.
Illustrate the British respect for traditional Indian governmental structures.

Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2


The emergence of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) represents perhaps the most significant evolution in monetary systems since
the abandonment of the gold standard. Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, which operate on decentralized networks and derive their
value from market speculation and network effects, CBDCs are digital representations of a nation’s fiat currency, backed by the full faith
and credit of the issuing government. This fundamental distinction has profound implications for monetary policy, financial stability, and
the very nature of money itself.


The potential benefits of CBDCs are compelling. They could dramatically reduce the costs associated with printing, distributing, and
securing physical currency, while providing governments with unprecedented real-time visibility into economic transactions. This granular
data could revolutionize monetary policy implementation, allowing central banks to adjust interest rates and money supply with surgical
precision based on actual spending patterns rather than lagged economic indicators. Furthermore, CBDCs could extend financial services
to underbanked populations, providing secure, government-backed digital payment systems without requiring traditional banking
infrastructure.


However, the implementation of CBDCs raises profound concerns about privacy, surveillance, and individual autonomy. Unlike cash
transactions, which are inherently anonymous, CBDC transactions would be traceable and recordable by the issuing authority. This
capability could enable unprecedented government surveillance of individual spending patterns, potentially chilling free expression and
political dissent. The programmable nature of digital currencies also raises dystopian possibilities: governments could theoretically
impose expiration dates on money, restrict its use for certain purchases, or even freeze individual accounts instantly based on political or
social criteria.


The international implications are equally complex. CBDCs could challenge the dominance of the US dollar in international trade,
particularly if major economies like China successfully implement their digital yuan for cross-border transactions. This could
fundamentally alter global power dynamics and reduce America’s ability to enforce economic sanctions. Conversely, the network effects

inherent in digital payment systems might create new forms of monetary hegemony, where the first-mover advantage in CBDC
implementation translates into disproportionate influence over global financial architecture.


(430 words | Adapted from: The Economist, “Central Bank Digital Currencies: Promise and Peril”)

options: Emphasize the revolutionary magnitude of the CBDC development.
Establish the historical precedent for major monetary system changes.
Suggest that CBDCs represent a return to commodity-backed currency.
Highlight the cyclical nature of monetary policy evolution.

The emergence of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) represents perhaps the most significant evolution in monetary systems since
the abandonment of the gold standard. Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, which operate on decentralized networks and derive their
value from market speculation and network effects, CBDCs are digital representations of a nation’s fiat currency, backed by the full faith
and credit of the issuing government. This fundamental distinction has profound implications for monetary policy, financial stability, and
the very nature of money itself.


The potential benefits of CBDCs are compelling. They could dramatically reduce the costs associated with printing, distributing, and
securing physical currency, while providing governments with unprecedented real-time visibility into economic transactions. This granular
data could revolutionize monetary policy implementation, allowing central banks to adjust interest rates and money supply with surgical
precision based on actual spending patterns rather than lagged economic indicators. Furthermore, CBDCs could extend financial services

infrastructure.

transactions, which are inherently anonymous, CBDC transactions would be traceable and recordable by the issuing authority. This
capability could enable unprecedented government surveillance of individual spending patterns, potentially chilling free expression and
political dissent. The programmable nature of digital currencies also raises dystopian possibilities: governments could theoretically
impose expiration dates on money, restrict its use for certain purchases, or even freeze individual accounts instantly based on political or
social criteria.

particularly if major economies like China successfully implement their digital yuan for cross-border transactions. This could
fundamentally alter global power dynamics and reduce America’s ability to enforce economic sanctions. Conversely, the network effects

inherent in digital payment systems might create new forms of monetary hegemony, where the first-mover advantage in CBDC

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 3


The hard problem of consciousness, as formulated by philosopher David Chalmers, represents perhaps the most intractable challenge in
contemporary philosophy of mind. While neuroscience has made remarkable progress in mapping the neural correlates of consciousness
and explaining the functional aspects of mental processes-what Chalmers terms the “easy problems”-the question of why there is
something it is like to have subjective experiences remains stubbornly resistant to scientific explanation. This explanatory gap between
objective neural activity and subjective phenomenal experience strikes at the heart of our understanding of the relationship between mind
and matter.


The conventional materialist approach assumes that consciousness emerges from complex neural interactions in much the same way
that wetness emerges from H2O molecules. However, this analogy fails to capture the uniqueness of the consciousness problem. While
we can fully explain wetness in terms of molecular behavior without any residual mystery, consciousness presents what philosophers call
the “qualitative” or “phenomenal” aspects of experience-the redness of red, the painfulness of pain, or the taste of chocolate-that seem to
resist reduction to purely physical descriptions. These qualia appear to possess an irreducible subjective dimension that cannot be
captured by objective scientific methodology.


Several theoretical frameworks have emerged to address this challenge. Integrated Information Theory (IIT), developed by Giulio Tononi,
proposes that consciousness corresponds to integrated information (?) in a system, suggesting that any system with sufficient integrated
information will be conscious. This theory makes the counterintuitive prediction that certain artificial systems or even collections of
photodiodes could possess consciousness. Global Workspace Theory, championed by Bernard Baars, focuses on the functional
architecture of consciousness, proposing that conscious experiences arise when information becomes globally accessible across
different brain modules. Panpsychism, increasingly defended by philosophers like Philip Goff, takes the radical step of proposing that
consciousness is a fundamental feature of reality, present even in elementary particles.


Yet each of these approaches faces significant challenges. IIT struggles with its implication that isolated systems could be highly
conscious, potentially leading to a consciousness explosion in complex networks. Global Workspace Theory, while functionally elegant,
doesn’t obviously bridge the explanatory gap between access and phenomenal experience. Panpsychism faces the combination problem:
how do micro-conscious entities combine to create unified conscious experiences? The persistence of these difficulties suggests that our
current conceptual frameworks may be fundamentally inadequate for understanding consciousness, requiring either revolutionary
scientific breakthroughs or radical philosophical reconceptualization.


(430 words | Adapted from: Philip Goff, Galileo’s Error: Foundations for a New Science of Mind)

options: The complexity of neural mechanisms underlying conscious experience.
The persistent failure of scientific methods to explain subjective experience.
The philosophical resistance to accepting materialist explanations.
The technical limitations of current neuroscientific research methods.

Passage – 4


She had always been suspicious of happiness, the way it arrived unannounced and settled into the corners of her life like dust that would
inevitably need sweeping away. Margaret watched her daughter Clara arrange flowers in the crystal vase-white roses, baby’s breath,
eucalyptus-with the methodical precision of someone who believed that beauty could be imposed upon chaos through careful attention to
detail. The afternoon light streaming through the kitchen window caught the water droplets on the petals, creating tiny prisms that
scattered rainbow fragments across the marble countertop.


“You don’t have to stay,” Clara said, not looking up from her arrangement. “I know you have your book club.”


But Margaret couldn’t leave, not yet. There was something about the quality of light, the particular way Clara’s hands moved among the
flowers, the almost religious concentration on her daughter’s face that made her want to memorize this moment before it dissolved into

the ordinary succession of minutes that comprised their days. She had learned, after David’s death, that happiness-real happiness, not the
manufactured kind that came in greeting cards and pharmaceutical advertisements-was always borrowed time, always subject to
revocation without notice.


Clara stepped back to assess her work, tilting her head with the same gesture she had made as a child when puzzling over jigsaw pieces
or math problems. The resemblance to David in that moment was so sharp that Margaret felt her breath catch. But instead of the familiar
ache of loss, she experienced something else: a recognition that grief and joy were not opposites but rather different faces of the same
deep capacity for love, different ways of measuring what mattered.


“They’re beautiful,” Margaret said, and meant it in ways that encompassed more than flowers.


Clara smiled-not the careful, protective smile she had worn for months after the funeral, but something genuine and unguarded. “I thought
we might have people over again. Small dinners, nothing elaborate. What do you think?”


Margaret nodded, understanding that this was not really about dinner parties but about Clara’s tentative willingness to reengage with life,
to risk the vulnerability that came with opening one’s door and heart to others. The flowers were not merely decoration but declaration: we
are ready to create beauty again, ready to believe in the possibility of celebration even in the shadow of loss.


The late afternoon sun shifted, and the prisms on the counter scattered into ordinary water droplets. But something had changed in the
quality of the silence between them, something that felt like permission-to hope, to plan, to trust in the reliability of small joys even when
larger sorrows remained unresolved.


(510 words | Original Fiction for CLAT Practice)

options: Her belief that happiness is inherently temporary and fragile.
Margaret’s compulsive need to control her environment.
Her association of cleanliness with emotional well-being.
Her tendency to find fault with positive experiences.

eucalyptus-with the methodical precision of someone who believed that beauty could be imposed upon chaos through careful attention to
detail. The afternoon light streaming through the kitchen window caught the water droplets on the petals, creating tiny prisms that
scattered rainbow fragments across the marble countertop.


“You don’t have to stay,” Clara said, not looking up from her arrangement. “I know you have your book club.”


But Margaret couldn’t leave, not yet. There was something about the quality of light, the particular way Clara’s hands moved among the
flowers, the almost religious concentration on her daughter’s face that made her want to memorize this moment before it dissolved into

the ordinary succession of minutes that comprised their days. She had learned, after David’s death, that happiness-real happiness, not the
manufactured kind that came in greeting cards and pharmaceutical advertisements-was always borrowed time, always subject to
revocation without notice.


Clara stepped back to assess her work, tilting her head with the same gesture she had made as a child when puzzling over jigsaw pieces
or math problems. The resemblance to David in that moment was so sharp that Margaret felt her breath catch. But instead of the familiar
ache of loss, she experienced something else: a recognition that grief and joy were not opposites but rather different faces of the same
deep capacity for love, different ways of measuring what mattered.


“They’re beautiful,” Margaret said, and meant it in ways that encompassed more than flowers.


Clara smiled-not the careful, protective smile she had worn for months after the funeral, but something genuine and unguarded. “I thought
we might have people over again. Small dinners, nothing elaborate. What do you think?”


Margaret nodded, understanding that this was not really about dinner parties but about Clara’s tentative willingness to reengage with life,
to risk the vulnerability that came with opening one’s door and heart to others. The flowers were not merely decoration but declaration: we
are ready to create beauty again, ready to believe in the possibility of celebration even in the shadow of loss.


The late afternoon sun shifted, and the prisms on the counter scattered into ordinary water droplets. But something had changed in the
quality of the silence between them, something that felt like permission-to hope, to plan, to trust in the reliability of small joys even when
larger sorrows remained unresolved.

options: Her attempt to control grief through ritual and routine.
The artificial nature of trying to create beauty after loss.
Her methodical approach to rebuilding a meaningful life.
The fragility of domestic happiness in the face of mortality.

Directions for questions 25 to 52: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


US President Donald Trump suggested that Cuba could be the next target of American military action, even as he referred to recent US
operations involving Venezuela and Iran. Speaking at the Future Investment Initiative conference in Miami, Florida, Trump said, “Cuba is
next, by the way-but pretend I didn’t say that. Please, please, please, media, disregard that statement. Thank you very much. Cuba’s next.”
The remarks come after the US military raided Venezuela and forcibly seized its president, Nicolás Maduro, on January 3, and launched
ongoing large-scale joint attacks with Israel on Iran on February 28, according to Xinhua news agency. Cuba has been facing a severe
economic and energy crisis due to decades of US sanctions. The United Nations has warned that fuel shortages are pushing the country
towards a humanitarian crisis. Earlier this month, Trump had said Cuba is likely to “fall pretty soon”, but added that his administration
would focus on Iran “right now”. Trump also sharply criticised NATO, calling it a “paper tiger” and questioning whether Washington should
continue defending allies that, he said, failed to support the United States in times of need. Speaking at the Future Investment Initiative
Priority Summit in Miami, he said the alliance had not backed the US when it mattered. “NATO is a paper tiger… They didn’t come to our
aid,” he said. In unusually blunt remarks, Trump suggested a reassessment of US commitments to the alliance. “Why would we be there for
them if they’re not there for us?” he said, describing NATO’s response as a “tremendous mistake”. He also recounted conversations with
European leaders, including French President Emmanuel Macron, saying offers of support came only after military action had concluded.
“As soon as the war is over, we will send ships,” Trump quoted Macron as saying, adding, “I don’t want them when the war is over.”

It was a joint military operation conducted by the United States and Israel targeting Iranian military and nuclear assets.
It was a defensive operation conducted by Iran against foreign intervention.
It was conducted under the mandate of the United Nations.

Passage – 2


Twelve years after the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh, the Rajya Sabha passed the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill,
clearing the way for Amaravati to be officially incorporated as the sole capital of Andhra Pradesh, with effect from June 2, 2024. The Bill
received near-unanimous support across political parties in the Upper House, with the notable exception of the YSR Congress Party
(YSRCP), whose MPs opposed it, arguing that the Bill ignored the demands of farmers in the area. The debate was initiated by senior
Congress MP Renuka Chowdhury, who criticised the 12-year delay, calling it a “statement of national shame” and questioning why it took
so long to fulfil a commitment made on the floor of the House. Union Minister and Telugu Desam Party (TDP) leader K. Rammohan Naidu

welcomed the development, saying it redefined the pride, faith and consciousness of the country in its democracy and leadership. In
essence, the passage of the Bill formally puts to rest years of uncertainty over Andhra Pradesh’s capital following its split from Telangana
in 2014, finally giving the State a constitutionally recognised, single capital city in Amaravati.


When Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy and the YSRCP came to power in 2019, they proposed a controversial Three-Capital Model for Andhra
Pradesh, citing regional balance and financial viability as key reasons. The three capitals proposed were:
• Visakhapatnam as the Executive/Administrative Capital
• Amaravati as the Legislative Capital
• Kurnool as the Judicial Capital


More recently, even as the Amaravati Bill was being passed in Parliament, Jagan proposed that instead of Amaravati, a “capital corridor”
named MAVIGAN should be formed by combining Vijayawada, Guntur, and Machilipatnam. Jagan claimed that the MAVIGUN model could
save up to Rs. 1.9 lakh crore compared to the Amaravati project.

options: Kurnool
Hyderabad
Chennai
Vijayawada

Passage – 3


The central government notified a 4 per cent retail inflation target with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points on either side for a five-year
period from April 1, 2026, to March 31, 2031. According to a gazette notification issued by the Department of Economic Affairs under
Section 45ZA of the RBI Act, 1934, the upper tolerance limit has been fixed at 6 per cent, while the lower limit is set at 2 per cent. The
decision has been taken in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), retaining the existing inflation-targeting framework. This
marks the second consecutive extension of the same target, after it was first introduced in 2016 and later continued in 2021. The
framework formally mandates the RBI to maintain inflation around 4 per cent, with flexibility within the 2-6 per cent band. India adopted
the flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework in 2016, with the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), headed by the RBI
Governor, tasked with setting policy rates to achieve this objective. Over the past decade, inflation has remained within the prescribed
band for roughly three-fourths of the time, although volatility increased during the pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Recent data
shows retail inflation rose to 3.21 percent in February from 2.74 per cent in the previous month. The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) is
based on a revised series with 2024 as the base year. Ahead of this notification, the RBI had released a discussion paper in August 2025
seeking stakeholder feedback on key aspects of the inflation framework. These included whether headline or core inflation should guide
policy, whether the 4 per cent target remains optimal, if the tolerance band needs revision, and whether a fixed target should be replaced
with a range. The RBI noted that the FIT framework has broadly performed well, with inflation averaging around 4 per cent in its early years
and stabilising again in recent years after a spike during global disruptions. It emphasised the need for policy certainty and credibility,
especially amid heightened global and domestic economic uncertainty.
content.questionText: Which of the following is responsible for setting interest rates in India to control inflation?
options: Finance Commission
NITI Aayog
Monetary Policy Committee
Ministry of Finance

India inducted its third nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN), INS Aridaman, significantly strengthening its sea-based
nuclear deterrent capabilities. The Indian Navy also commissioned the advanced stealth frigate INS Taragiri at a separate ceremony.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh presided over the commissioning ceremonies. The inductions signify a major enhancement in India’s
naval strength and maritime combat capabilities. At the commissioning ceremony of INS Taragiri, the fourth vessel of Project 17A of the
Nilgiri-class stealth guided-missile frigates, Singh said it is a unique platform, as it fits perfectly into every role - from high-intensity combat
to maritime security, anti-piracy operations to coastal surveillance, and humanitarian missions. With INS Aridaman’s induction, India will
have three operational ballistic missile submarines at sea for the first time. The indigenous SSBN is designed to carry more long-range
nuclear-tipped missiles than INS Arihant and INS Arighaat, which were commissioned in 2016 and 2024, respectively. A larger 7,000-tonne
vessel, INS Aridaman will carry more K-15 missiles, as well as the intermediate-range K-4 nuclear-capable submarine-launched ballistic
missiles (SLBM) - with nearly double the number of VLS tubes than its predecessors - that can hit targets 3,500 km away. A fourth SSBN is
currently under construction. India is also pursuing a nuclear-powered attack submarine (SSN) programme. The Navy plans to build two
SSNs indigenously and acquire one on lease from Russia, which is expected to arrive by 2027-28 and bridge the capability gap until India’s
own boats are ready. INS Aridaman will join its predecessors as a key component of India’s nuclear triad, which refers to a country’s ability
to launch nuclear missiles from platforms in the air, land, and at sea. India is part of a select group of countries with nuclear triad
capabilities. These include the United States, Russia and China.

options: It is smaller than INS Arihant
It carries fewer missiles than earlier submarines
It is a larger 7,000-tonne submarine with enhanced missile capacity
It is powered by diesel engines

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required to
choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 1


Part XIII of the Constitution of India encompasses provisions pertaining to the freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse within the

territorial bounds of India, delineated across Articles 301-307. While Article 301 establishes the overarching principle of freedom in trade
and intercourse, its application can be qualified by the limitations detailed in Articles 302-305. Dominantly, authority rests with the Union,
which holds the prerogative to impose reasonable restrictions in the public interest, thereby curtailing the freedom of trade or commerce.
Similarly, a State legislature is empowered to impose such restrictions, albeit necessitating the sanction of the President. Consequently,
the Union exercises control over the State legislature. Chapter XIII endeavours to forge India into a cohesive economic entity for trade and
commerce, centrally overseen by the Union.


Article 301 stipulates: “Subject to the other provisions of this Part, trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall
be free.” The “freedom” articulated under Article 301 can be construed as the entitlement to unrestricted movement of persons or goods,
whether tangible or intangible, commercial or non-commercial, without hindrance from barriers, whether inter-State, intra-State, or any
other impediment functioning as such barriers. Under Article 301, the term ‘trade’ signifies a genuine, substantial, systematic, or organised
course of activity or conduct with a defined purpose.


As per article 302, Parliament may by law impose such restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce or intercourse between one State
and another or within any part of the territory of India as may be required in the public interest. Another exception to article 301, is article
304 that allows State Legislatures to:
Restrictions on trade, commerce and intercourse among States.
(a) States may impose taxes on goods imported from other States or Union Territories only if similar goods produced within the State are
taxed equally.
(b) A State may impose reasonable restrictions on trade in the public interest, but such a law requires the President’s prior sanction.
But such Tax cannot be used to favour local manufacturers at the cost of outside goods.
content.questionText:
M is a trader who transports processed food items from Karnataka to Gujarat. The Gujarat government issued a new rule
requiring all out-of-state food consignments to pay a “Special Entry Processing Fee” of Rs.8,000 per truck, in addition to normal taxes, to
“check quality compliance.” The fee is not charged on goods produced within Gujarat, even though they undergo the same quality checks.
M challenges the rule as violating freedom of trade and commerce under Article 301. Which of the following is the legally correct
position?
options: The rule is valid because states have complete autonomy to regulate trade inside their territory.
The rule is unconstitutional because it creates a discriminatory barrier against goods coming from outside the state.
The rule is valid because Article 301 protects only inter-state movement of people.
The rule is valid because quality-checking requirements always fall under “regulatory measures,”.

A motion is a formal idea by a member to do something. Its objectives form the basis of the collective decision-making process. It helps to
focus the attention of the group. So that issue by-issue decisions can be taken in an orderly manner in the larger assembly. Generally, a
proposition must be expressed in a way to perform an action or to express an opinion. A motion to do nothing should not be offered if the
same result can be had without doing anything. If the Assembly does not want to do so, such a proposal may lead to confusion. Some of
the motions used in parliament are:


(a) A Substantive Motion is an independent, self-contained proposal submitted for the approval of a Legislative House or Assembly,
drafted to express a decision or opinion. The motion entails a debate followed by a compulsory vote if the notice is accepted and the
motion is moved.

(b) Adjournment motion is brought in the House to discuss any serious and important problem of the country. For discussion on this, all
the regular proceedings of the House are stopped i.e. adjourned. The purpose of the adjournment motion is to take the government to task
for any recent lapse or failure of the government, which has serious consequences. Its acceptance is considered as a condemnation of
the government.


(c) The term ‘Parliamentary Privilege’ means certain rights and immunities which each House of Parliament and its Committees have
collectively and members of each House individually, without which they would not be able to discharge their functions efficiently and
effectively. The purpose of parliamentary privileges is to protect the independence, authority and dignity of Parliament.


(d) No Confidence Motion is passed when an opposition party in the Lok Sabha feels that the government does not have a majority or has
lost the confidence of the government in the house, it brings a no-confidence motion. Article-75 of the Indian Constitution states that the
Union Council of Ministers is answerable to the Lok Sabha. The Council of Ministers including the Prime Minister have to resign if the
motion of no confidence is passed against it.


(e) Substitute Motions-Motions moved in substitution of the original motion for taking into consideration a policy or situation or statement
or any other matter are called substitute motions. Such motions, though drafted in such a way as to be capable of expressing an opinion
by themselves are not, strictly speaking, substantive motions in as much as they depend upon the original motion.


(f) Subsidiary Motions-They depend upon or relate to other motion or follow upon some proceedings in the House. They by themselves
have no meaning and are not capable of stating the decision of the House without reference to the original motion or proceedings of the
House.


(g) A Censure Motion is a motion moved to express strong disapproval of specific policies or actions of the Government. Unlike a No
Confidence Motion, its passage does not necessarily require the resignation of the Council of Ministers.


(h) A Privilege Motion is moved when a member believes that a breach of parliamentary privilege has occurred. A breach of privilege
includes any act that obstructs the functioning of the House or its members, including deliberately misleading the House.

The Opposition in the Lok Sabha is outraged over a sudden and massive data breach in a government-run healthcare portal that
leaked the private records of millions of citizens. Mr. X, a member of the Opposition, wants to move a motion that specifically names the
Minister of Electronics and Information Technology for “gross negligence and failure of policy.” He also wants to ensure that while the
House expresses its strong disapproval, the government remains in power so that the ongoing budget session is not collapsed.
Which motion should Mr. X ideally move to achieve his specific objective?

No-Confidence Motion, because it is the strongest way to show that the House is unhappy with the government’s handling of the data
breach.

Censure Motion, because it can be directed at a specific minister and expresses disapproval of a policy without forcing the resignation of

regular business

situation’ given notice of by Shri E Minister of State for External Affairs was admitted and listed for discussion in the House. Shri J

Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required to
choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.

Passage – 3


The Supreme Court in Ashok Saxena v. State of Uttarakhand explained the scope of the Doctrine of Transfer of Malice (Transmigration of
Motive) as embodied in Section 301 IPC. The doctrine provides that when an accused intends to kill or cause fatal harm to one person but
instead kills another, unintended person in the course of the same act, the original intention is legally transferred to the actual victim. Thus,
the absence of a specific intention toward the deceased does not absolve the accused of liability for murder. A fundamental idea in
criminal law is the doctrine of transfer of malice, which focuses primarily on the concept of mens rea, or the guilty mind. It deals with
situations in which a person intends to commit a crime against one person but accidentally causes harm to another. Although commonly
applied in cases of murder under criminal law, this principle reflects a broader idea that intention may, in certain circumstances, be
attributed to unintended consequences depending on the nature of the act and surrounding facts. When it comes to comprehending
criminal law’s application and the liability of an offender, this legal doctrine is crucial and holds significant importance in understanding the
liability of an offender and the application of criminal law..The doctrine of transferred malice is not defined anywhere in the Indian Penal
Code, but the essentials are given under Section 301(2) of the Indian Penal Code. According to section 301 of the Indian Penal Code, “if a
person does any act he knows or intends does any act which he knows or intends that is likely to cause death, he commits culpable
homicide, and by causing the death of any person, whose death he neither intends to nor knowns by himself that his act will cause the
death of that person. Some essentials of doctrine of transferred malice are:
• Cause the death of a human being.
• By doing an act with the intention or knowledge of causing the death of a person.
• Causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death.
• Cause the death of another person instead of the intended person.
content.questionText:
T administers poison in G’s morning cup, as he was the contender of other half of his ancestral property. G happily accepts the
morning cup and told T that he is considering to surrender the property his favor. T felt guilty of poisoning the tea, and asked G to not
have it, as he might have forgotten to add sugar. T took the cup in the kitchen, and prepared another tea for G. J, a servant in the house,
later had the poisoned tea and died. Decide whether T could be held liable for killing J.
options: T could be held liable for killing J, because he poisoned the tea.
T could be held liable for killing J, because he did not spill the poisoned tea.
T could not be held liable for killing J, because he did not intend to kill J.
T could not be held liable for killing anyone, because he had a change of heart right before committing the crime.

A, driven by a longstanding rivalry, fires a gun at B in a crowded marketplace with the intention of causing his death. At that very
moment, B suddenly bends down to tie his shoelaces, and the bullet instead strikes C, an unsuspecting passer-by who is unknown to A,
resulting in C’s death. During the trial, A contends that he cannot be held liable for C’s death, as he had no intention to harm C.
Which of the following best reflects the correct legal position?
options: A cannot be held liable for murder because he lacked intention toward C specifically.
A is liable for murder of C under the doctrine of transferred malice, as his intention to kill B transfers to the actual victim.
A is liable only for attempt to murder B, not for C’s death.

A is liable for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, because the doctrine of transferred malice does not apply to unintended
victims.

Surrogacy, in simpler terms, is a legal arrangement between parents intending to have a child and the surrogate mother. Surrogacy is
helpful for people who can’t have a baby on their own, but it can also lead to problems. Commercial surrogacy, where people pay for
someone to have their baby, is banned in India. The Surrogacy Regulation Act, 2021 allows only altruistic surrogacy, which means that the
surrogate mother cannot receive any compensation apart from the medical expenses incurred during pregnancy including insurance
coverage. Commercial surrogacy, where the surrogate is paid in cash or kind, is banned. Before the intended couple can proceed with the
surrogacy, they need to obtain two certificates - a certificate of essentiality and a certificate of eligibility - from a competent authority. To
obtain a certificate of essentiality, certain conditions must be met.
A couple is allowed to go for surrogacy to become parents only when:
• At least 5 years have been passed of having been married.
• The couple must have no living child, whether biological, adopted, or surrogate, except when their existing child is suffering from a life-
threatening genetic disorder, or is mentally/physically disabled
• The couple has to prove the essentiality and incapability of fertility by showing a certificate of it.
• They have to also undertake that abandonment of the child born out of surrogacy will not be done by the intending parents.


Conditions to be a surrogate mother are:
• The woman chosen for surrogacy must be a close relative of the parents who will take the child after the birth.

• It is essential that the Surrogate mother must be a married woman and should also have at least one child of her own.
• The age of the surrogate mother should be between the age of 25-35 years.
• She can go to become a surrogate mother only once and must possess a certificate of physical and mental fitness for surrogacy.
• There should have insurance coverage for the Surrogate mother for some time to cover a period of pregnancy as well as for the period
after that.
• The act also gives directions for the regulation of the functioning of surrogacy clinics. All surrogacy clinics in the country should be
registered.
• It also specifies that no sex selection can be done when it becomes to surrogacy.
content.questionText:
A and B were parents to K, who they adopted when he was 3 months old. K, was A’s sister’s son, who then legally gave him to A.
Recently with the introduction of surrogacy law, A and B were excited to have a daughter via surrogacy. They filled in all the formalities,
and chose a female relative that was ready to be a surrogate mother. Decide whether they can have a female child through surrogacy?
options: A and B already had an adopted child; hence they cannot be a surrogate parent.
A and B already had an adopted child, and since the child has their family lineage, they cannot be a surrogate parent.
A and B can have a surrogate daughter because they already have a male child.
A and B can have a surrogate daughter as they have the right to reproductive autonomy.

Indian citizenship is governed by the Citizenship Act, of 1955, a key piece of legislation that outlines how an individual can become a
citizen of India. With its roots in the Indian Constitution and updated over the years to reflect changing realities, this Act defines five main
ways to acquire Indian citizenship.


Citizenship by Birth: Anyone born in India between January 26, 1950, and June 30, 1987, is automatically considered an Indian citizen,
regardless of the nationality of their parents. For those born on or after July 1, 1987, at least one parent must be an Indian citizen at the
time of birth for the child to qualify as an Indian citizen.


Citizenship by Registration: Persons of Indian origin (PIO) who have been residing in India for at least seven years are eligible to apply. The
required residency period typically includes having lived in India continuously for the 12 months immediately before applying, as well as for
six out of the eight years preceding that period. Foreign nationals married to Indian citizens can apply for citizenship through registration if
they have been married and residing in India for a continuous period of seven years. Minor children of Indian citizens are eligible for
registration without any specific residency requirement. Individuals whose parents are or were Indian citizens are also eligible, even if born
outside India. In addition, persons who or whose parents were residents of undivided India before the partition and who are now residing
in India may qualify.


Citizenship by Descent: Citizenship by descent applies to individuals born outside India. If a person was born between January 26, 1950
and December 10, 1992, they are considered an Indian citizen if their father was an Indian citizen at the time of their birth. However, for
individuals born outside India after December 10, 1992, either parent must have been an Indian citizen at the time of the child’s birth.

Citizenship by Naturalization: To qualify, an applicant must have resided in India for at least 12 months immediately before the date of
application, and for an aggregate of 11 years in the 14 years preceding that 12-month period. The applicant must be of good character,
have adequate knowledge of at least one of the languages listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, and intend to reside in
India or serve the Indian government.


Citizenship by Incorporation of Territory: When a foreign territory becomes part of India through legal means-such as a treaty, cession, or
political agreement-the Government of India may, by order, specify the conditions under which the people of that territory are granted
Indian citizenship.

Ayesha was born in Mumbai in 1986. Her father is an Indian citizen, but her mother is a foreign national from France. In 2025,
Ayesha applies for a government job that requires proof of Indian citizenship. The authorities question whether she is an Indian citizen by
birth. Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, what is Ayesha’s correct legal status?
options: Ayesha is an Indian citizen by birth because she was born in India before 1 July 1987, and having at least one Indian parent is sufficient.
Ayesha is not an Indian citizen because both parents must be Indian citizens for children born after 1950.
Ayesha must apply for citizenship by registration since one parent is a foreign national.

Directions for questions 83 to 108: Read the passages and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2


The resurgence of ancient trade corridors through contemporary infrastructure projects represents a fundamental shift in global
commerce patterns. China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), launched in 2013, exemplifies this transformation by revitalizing the historic Silk
Road through massive investments in ports, railways, and digital connectivity across Asia, Europe, and Africa. However, this modernization
comes with significant geopolitical implications that extend beyond mere economic considerations.


The BRI’s infrastructure development has created new dependencies between participating nations and China, fundamentally altering
traditional power dynamics in international trade. Countries like Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and several African nations have accumulated
substantial debt obligations to Chinese lenders, leading to concerns about “debt-trap diplomacy” where strategic assets might be
surrendered when payments become unsustainable. The Hambantota Port in Sri Lanka, leased to China for 99 years after debt
restructuring, exemplifies these concerns.


Maritime chokepoints have become increasingly critical as trade volume expands along these new routes. The Strait of Malacca, through
which approximately 25% of global trade passes, represents a vulnerability that could disrupt supply chains across multiple continents.
Similarly, the Suez Canal’s temporary blockage by the Ever Given container ship in 2021 demonstrated how single infrastructure failures
can cascade into global economic disruption.


Digital trade corridors are emerging alongside physical infrastructure, creating parallel systems of data flow that mirror goods movement.
The Digital Silk Road component of the BRI includes fiber-optic cables, 5G networks, and data centers that enable real-time tracking and
management of cargo across vast distances. However, this digital integration raises concerns about data sovereignty and surveillance
capabilities that could compromise national security interests.


Environmental considerations increasingly influence route selection and development strategies. Climate change impacts on Arctic ice
coverage are opening new northern passages that could significantly reduce shipping times between Asia and Europe, potentially
undermining investments in southern routes. Meanwhile, carbon emission regulations in major markets are forcing logistics companies to
optimize routes for environmental efficiency rather than purely economic considerations.

Passage – 3


The recent revelations about match-fixing in international cricket have exposed a labyrinthine network of corruption that extends far
beyond individual players accepting bribes. The investigation uncovered a sophisticated ecosystem where betting syndicates, team
officials, broadcasters, and even ground staff collaborated to manipulate outcomes. What makes this scandal particularly insidious is not
merely the financial transactions, but the systematic erosion of sporting integrity through micro-manipulations that are virtually
undetectable to spectators.


The modus operandi involved players deliberately bowling wides or no-balls at predetermined overs, rather than fixing entire match results.
This approach minimized suspicion while maximizing profits for betting syndicates who could predict these specific events. The
investigation revealed that corrupt players received coded messages through social media platforms, with seemingly innocuous posts
containing instructions about when to execute these subtle infractions.


Perhaps most disturbing is the revelation that some broadcasting companies were complicit, adjusting camera angles to obscure certain
plays from viewers while ensuring betting partners could observe the manipulated actions. Ground maintenance crews were allegedly paid
to alter pitch conditions in specific areas, affecting ball trajectory in ways that favored predetermined outcomes without appearing
obviously artificial.


The psychological profile of involved players reveals a troubling pattern: most were not financially desperate but rather motivated by a
combination of peer pressure, normalized corruption within team hierarchies, and a gradual desensitization to ethical boundaries. Senior
players often initiated younger teammates through seemingly harmless requests, progressively involving them in more serious infractions.


Law enforcement agencies now face the challenge of prosecuting crimes that occurred across multiple jurisdictions with evidence that is
largely circumstantial. The betting syndicates operated through cryptocurrency transactions and encrypted communications, making
financial trails nearly impossible to trace. Moreover, the statute of limitations has expired for many earlier incidents, allowing key
perpetrators to escape legal consequences while the sport’s reputation suffers irreparable damage.
content.questionText: Which of the following can be most reasonably inferred about the nature of sports corruption described in the passage?
options: Financial desperation among players was the primary catalyst for widespread corruption practices
The corruption network’s sophistication suggests systematic institutional failures rather than isolated incidents
Broadcasting companies’ involvement was limited to passive observation of manipulated sporting events
Betting syndicates focused primarily on major match outcomes rather than specific micro-events

Passage – 4


Public outrage against figures such as Jeffrey Epstein has been widespread and justified. Yet a deeper question remains: why do some
among the wealthy and powerful assert themselves through domination and wrongdoing? What is it about power that encourages such
displays?

It is often argued that acts like sexual violence are less about desire and more about control. The philosopher Michel Foucault suggested
that such acts are not fundamentally different from other forms of physical assault, since both involve force imposed against another’s
will. When societies treat sexual crimes as distinct, they may reinforce norms of chastity and purity, thereby exerting a secondary form of
control over victims.


If power reproduces itself through humiliation, a deeper question arises: why does domination depend on moral injury? The philosopher
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel argued that human beings seek recognition of their moral worth, which is possible only through reciprocal
relations among equals. Forced submission cannot generate genuine respect, since fear and recognition cannot coexist.


The sociologist Andrew Sayer extends this argument by suggesting that elites replace broader solidarity with exclusive networks. These
relationships are not based on equality but on calculated exchanges of status and advantage. Cultural portrayals, such as The Apprentice,
show how such alliances often turn unstable when status changes. In such environments, recognition is distorted and expressed through
domination rather than equality.
content.questionText: Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: Power among elites depends on cooperation, stability, and ethically grounded relations.
Domination reflects the absence of genuine recognition and reciprocal relations.
Legal systems treat sexual crimes differently due to outdated moral norms.
Cultural narratives exaggerate instability within elite social networks.

Directions for questions 83 to 108: Read the passages and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 4


Public outrage against figures such as Jeffrey Epstein has been widespread and justified. Yet a deeper question remains: why do some
among the wealthy and powerful assert themselves through domination and wrongdoing? What is it about power that encourages such
displays?

It is often argued that acts like sexual violence are less about desire and more about control. The philosopher Michel Foucault suggested
that such acts are not fundamentally different from other forms of physical assault, since both involve force imposed against another’s
will. When societies treat sexual crimes as distinct, they may reinforce norms of chastity and purity, thereby exerting a secondary form of
control over victims.


If power reproduces itself through humiliation, a deeper question arises: why does domination depend on moral injury? The philosopher
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel argued that human beings seek recognition of their moral worth, which is possible only through reciprocal
relations among equals. Forced submission cannot generate genuine respect, since fear and recognition cannot coexist.


The sociologist Andrew Sayer extends this argument by suggesting that elites replace broader solidarity with exclusive networks. These
relationships are not based on equality but on calculated exchanges of status and advantage. Cultural portrayals, such as The Apprentice,
show how such alliances often turn unstable when status changes. In such environments, recognition is distorted and expressed through
domination rather than equality.
content.questionText: According to the passage, Foucault’s argument implies that sexual violence is:
options: A morally distinct offence rooted in violations of chastity and social norms.
Primarily an expression of desire that becomes criminal when social order breaks.
Comparable to other forms of violence involving force imposed against another.
A unique category of crime requiring specialised legal and ethical treatment.

Directions for questions 109 to 114: Answer the questions on the basis of the information given below.


Silicon chip production is concentrated in a few technologically advanced economies such as Taiwan, South Korea, and the USA, which
dominate fabrication capacity and high-end semiconductor manufacturing. These chips are essential inputs for industries including
electronics, automobiles, and telecommunications. Countries like India and Germany rely heavily on imports to meet domestic demand.
Global trade in semiconductors is influenced by geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions, and strategic policies, making chip
production and export control critical factors in economic and national security planning worldwide.


Four countries—Taiwan, South Korea, the USA, and China—are major producers of silicon chips, while the three major importers are India,
Germany, and Brazil. In the year 2025, production levels were as follows: Taiwan produced 600 million units, South Korea 400 million units,
the USA 300 million units, and China 200 million units. Taiwan, South Korea, the USA, and China export 80%, 75%, 60%, and 50% of their
production, respectively. Out of their total exports, each country secretly reserves a portion for a mysterious new importer, “Zura,” which is
not included in the list of importing countries. Taiwan reserves one-third of its exports for Zura, South Korea reserves 40%, the USA 20%,
and China 25%. China exports equal quantities to each of the three importing countries. 50% of the remaining exports from Taiwan are
sent to India.


Brazil imports a total of 145 million silicon chips, with imports from Taiwan, South Korea, and the USA in the ratio 7 : 3 : 2. The ratio of
South Korea’s exports to India and Germany is 2 : 1, respectively. India’s imports from the USA are 44 million more than Germany’s imports
from the USA.
content.questionText: What was the total quantity of silicon chips (in million units) imported by Zura in 2025?

A company operates in three segments A, B, and C. In 2022, the total revenue of the company was Rs. 240 lakhs. Segment A contributed
40% of the total revenue, while the ratio of revenues of segments B and C was 5:3. In 2023, the total revenue increased by 25% of the
previous year. However, segment A’s revenue increased by only 10%, while segment B’s revenue increased by 40%. The remaining revenue
belonged to segment C.


The company’s total cost in 2022 was 60% of its revenue. Segment-wise cost distribution in 2022 was such that A, B, and C had costs in
the ratio 4:3:2. In 2023, overall cost increased by 25% of the previous year. However, cost of segment A increased by 30%, and cost of
segment B increased by 10%. The cost of segment C was the remaining amount.


Profit is defined as Revenue - Cost and profit margin is defined as Profit/Revenue × 100. Additionally, a performance bonus is allocated
only to segments where profit margin exceeds 25%.
content.questionText: What was the revenue (in Rs. Lakhs) of segment B in 2022?

Passage – 1


"Oh, Nastenka, Nastenka! Do you know how far you have reconciled me to myself? Do you know now that I shall not think so ill of myself,
as I have at some moments? Do you know that, maybe, I shall leave off grieving over the crime and sin of my life? for such a life is a crime
and a sin. And do not imagine that I have been exaggerating anything - for goodness' sake don't think that, Nastenka: for at times such

Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2


Every winter, a small miracle takes place across the Indian sky. High above the snow peaks of the Himalayas, at altitudes where even
planes struggle to breathe, flocks of bar-headed geese glide southward from the frozen lakes of Central Asia. They descend into the
wetlands of India (the Ganga plains) honking softly as they rest on the waters that have awaited them since Vedic times. This is the hamsa
of Indian imagination, the bird of Saraswati, the emblem of wisdom, purity, and transcendence.... But somewhere in the last two centuries,
the Indian goose was eclipsed.

In colonial translations, it was transformed into a European swan, a bird that never flew over the Himalayas, never nested in Ladakh, never
knew our monsoons. The goose carved in stone on temple walls was ignored and everyone paid attention to swans appearing next to
Shakuntala, transforming her into the Greek Leda.


In art and sculpture, friezes of 12th-century temples at Belur, Khajuraho, and Konark show the bird carved beside Saraswati, with a blunt
beak, rounded body, and webbed feet. This was India's own sacred bird - born of her rivers, not borrowed from Europe's ponds. To the
Europeans, the hamsa resembled the swan of their myths - so Saraswati's companion was Europeanised and deemed more elegant than
the ugly goose. The swan was like a ballet dancer; the goose was the squat Indian nautch girl.


The change seemed innocent, even poetic. But this mistranslation was not without consequence. ..Over time, the bar-headed goose - once
the bird of the Himalayas - was exiled from its own mythology. This was colonisation of imagination. We rejected the bird that actually flew
over our skies in favour of one imported through colonial eyes. The swan became Sanskritised, while the goose was forgotten.


Modern education separates zoology from literature. Children are not told that Saraswati's goose is among the most extraordinary
creatures on earth. It flies over the Himalayas at heights above 25,000ft, where oxygen is one-third of normal levels. Scientists still marvel
at its lungs and blood chemistry. It flies at night, in formation, gliding on thin air, carrying no luggage except memory. Its annual journey,
from the salt lakes of Tibet to the flooded plains of India, has continued unbroken for millennia. To call the hansa a swan is to erase
geography from faith.


The orthodox Hindu who insists on painting Saraswati on a swan repeats a colonial error, mistaking imported iconography for authenticity.
But the temples tell a different story. On their 800-year-old walls, the hamsa looks like what it truly is - a goose, not a swan.


(428 words, Column by Devdutt Pattanaik, The Hindu)
content.questionText: From the above lines it can be assumed that:
options: Colonial translations reshaped Indian religious imagery.
Swans historically migrated across Himalayan wetlands.
Saraswati originally symbolized European aesthetics exclusively.
Temples deliberately avoided depicting sacred birds.
