content.passageText:
Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 4


One of the most fascinating developments in modern science is the surprising discovery of recent decades that the laws of physics are
fine tuned for life. This means that, for life to be possible, certain numbers in physics had to fall within an incredibly narrow range. Like
Goldilocks's porridge, these numbers had to be just right, not too big and not too small.


Perhaps the most striking case is that of the cosmological constant, the number that measures the force that powers the accelerating
expansion of the universe. The cosmological constant is an odd number: it's extremely small but non-zero. You don't tend to find
fundamental constants with that kind of value. But it's a good job that it does. Because, if the cosmological constant were a bit bigger,
everything would have been forced apart so rapidly that no two particles would ever have met. We would have no stars, no planets nor any
kind of structural complexity. On the other hand, if the cosmological constant was less than zero, it would have added to gravity, meaning
that the entire universe would have collapsed back on itself within a split second. For life to be possible, this number had to be in the

strange, highly specific category it in fact occupies: extremely close to zero without crossing over into the negative. There are many other
examples of finely tuned constants in current physics.


Fundamentally, we face a choice. Either:
it's a coincidence that, of all the possible values that the finely tuned constants of physics may have had, they just happen to have the right
values for life;
or:
the constants have those values because they are right for life.


The former option is wildly improbable; on a conservative estimate, the odds of getting finely tuned constants by chance is less than 1 in
10 to the power (-136). The latter option amounts to a belief that something at the fundamental level of reality is directed towards the
emergence of life. I call this kind of fundamental goal-directedness 'cosmic purpose'.


(336 words, extracted from The Aeon)

Scientific debate focuses on whether physical constants are determined by necessity rather than chance alone.
The universe appears finely calibrated for life, raising the question whether this precision is accidental or purposeful.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 5


Imagine for a moment that you are not a human with discerning media habits. Instead you have been turned into a gazelle and have just
spotted a predator. Your first instinct would be to quickly get back into the car, until you remember that you are a gazelle and cannot drive.
Your second instinct would be to run away as fast as possible. You would probably not choose to bounce up and down with all four legs
extended, using up energy while making yourself visible to the thing that wants to eat you. And yet "stotting"-or, even more delightfully,
"pronking"-is a behaviour that gazelles and other prey animals routinely exhibit.


Why they do so is a matter of debate among biologists. It may well be a useful signal to the predator: that an animal is sufficiently fit and
healthy that it's not going to be easy to catch, or that the source of danger has been seen. It might be for a different audience: a signal that
a specimen with this much energy is going to make another gazelle very happy. But it entails risks, too: gazelles tend to skip stotting and
start scarpering when a predator gets sufficiently close.


The idea of costly signalling-incurring a penalty of some kind in order to send a message-is not just of interest to evolutionary biologists.
The human equivalents of pronking are important in workplaces, too.


If a manager wants to thank a team member for their work, for example, there are various options. They can send a quick text or email. Or
they can use an employee-engagement platform to send an industrialised message of appreciation. These options are a lot better than
silence, and they have the advantage of being quick. But nothing beats a handwritten note for the very reason that it is inconvenient.
Someone has taken the time and trouble to do something wildly countercultural: find a pen and paper, write a note, perhaps even put it in
an envelope. The costs that handwriting impose on the sender produce a clear signal that they really are grateful.


(351 words, extracted from The Economist)

options:
Seemingly wasteful or risky actions can function as credible signals of strength, awareness, or sincerity in both animal survival behaviour
and human social interactions.

Gazelles perform stotting mainly to display reproductive fitness, showing that survival behaviour in prey species is driven more by mating
competition than predator avoidance.

Workplace appreciation is most effective when expressed through traditional methods, suggesting that handwritten communication is
inherently superior to quick digital messages of thanks.

Predators are discouraged from pursuing prey that make conspicuous movements, because such displays confuse attackers and reduce
the likelihood of a successful chase.

quality of indigenous models developed with frugal innovation. Framing these developments within the broader vision of Prime Minister
Shri Narendra Modi for "Viksit Bharat" by 2047, he positioned the Summit as a decisive step toward building long-term technological and
semiconductor capacity in India.

Directions for questions 25 to 52: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2

Several countries which have signed up to Donald Trump's Board of Peace have contributed more than $7bn (£5.2bn) towards a Gaza
"relief package", the US president has said. Trump made the announcement during the first meeting of the organisation that many of US's
Western allies have refused to join, fearing the body originally meant to help end the war between Israel and Hamas may be intended to
replace the UN. The second phase of a US-brokered Gaza ceasefire plan includes the disarmament of Hamas and the reconstruction of
Gaza. It "looks like" Hamas would disarm, Trump told participants. However, there are few signs of the Palestinian group disarming.
Gazans say it is extending its control over the Strip. Speaking as the Board of Peace convened, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
said Israel had "agreed with our ally the US there will be no reconstruction of Gaza before the demilitarisation of Gaza".


The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251
others were taken hostage. Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 72,000
people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry. The enclave's economy is in ruins, with its buildings and
infrastructure largely destroyed. The UN estimates the cost of damage at $70bn. Countries including the UK, Canada, France and Germany
have refused to join the Board of Peace that came into being last month. In an effort to address concerns that the organisation was meant
as a way of sidelining the UN, Trump told the board's first meeting in Washington that "we're going to be working with the United Nations
very closely, we're going to bring them back". Gaza, the US president said, was "no longer a hotbed of radicalism and terror". "And to end
that, we have today, and I'm pleased to announce that Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, UAE, Morocco, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan, and
Kuwait have all contributed more than $7bn toward the relief package". "Every dollar spent is an investment in stability," he said, adding
that the UN would contribute $2bn for humanitarian assistance, while football body FIFA would raise $75m for soccer-related projects in
the Strip.

options: Geneva
New York
Brussels
Washington

Several countries which have signed up to Donald Trump's Board of Peace have contributed more than $7bn (£5.2bn) towards a Gaza
"relief package", the US president has said. Trump made the announcement during the first meeting of the organisation that many of US's
Western allies have refused to join, fearing the body originally meant to help end the war between Israel and Hamas may be intended to
replace the UN. The second phase of a US-brokered Gaza ceasefire plan includes the disarmament of Hamas and the reconstruction of
Gaza. It "looks like" Hamas would disarm, Trump told participants. However, there are few signs of the Palestinian group disarming.
Gazans say it is extending its control over the Strip. Speaking as the Board of Peace convened, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
said Israel had "agreed with our ally the US there will be no reconstruction of Gaza before the demilitarisation of Gaza".


The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251
others were taken hostage. Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 72,000
people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry. The enclave's economy is in ruins, with its buildings and
infrastructure largely destroyed. The UN estimates the cost of damage at $70bn. Countries including the UK, Canada, France and Germany
have refused to join the Board of Peace that came into being last month. In an effort to address concerns that the organisation was meant
as a way of sidelining the UN, Trump told the board's first meeting in Washington that "we're going to be working with the United Nations
very closely, we're going to bring them back". Gaza, the US president said, was "no longer a hotbed of radicalism and terror". "And to end
that, we have today, and I'm pleased to announce that Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, UAE, Morocco, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan, and
Kuwait have all contributed more than $7bn toward the relief package". "Every dollar spent is an investment in stability," he said, adding
that the UN would contribute $2bn for humanitarian assistance, while football body FIFA would raise $75m for soccer-related projects in
the Strip.

The Sixteenth Finance Commission (16th FC) has recommended that the Central Government retain the 41% share of tax devolution to the
States that had been implemented since 2021. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, in her Budget 2026 speech on February 1, 2026,
announced that the Centre has accepted the 16th FC's recommendations. "The Government has accepted the recommendation of the
Commission to retain the vertical share of devolution at 41%," Ms. Sitharaman said. "As recommended by the Commission, I have provided
Rs.1.4 lakh crore to the States for the FY 2026-27 as Finance Commission Grants. These include Rural and Urban Local Body and Disaster
Management Grants." The 16th FC was formally constituted on December 31, 2023, under the chairmanship of Arvind Panagariya, with the
task of making recommendations for the five-year period April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2031. It submitted its report to the President of India
on November 17, 2025, which was tabled in Parliament by Ms. Sitharaman on Sunday (February 1, 2026). The report of the 16th FC noted
that the "only instrument" available to the Finance Commission to assist the finances of the Union government was its share in the
divisible pool. It said that there was no further space to cut the States' share in the divisible pool as the Centre's cesses and surcharges -
not sharable with the States - had "cut" the size of the divisible pool from 89.1% of gross tax revenues in 2014-15 to a 74 80% during the
2020-24 period for which actuals figures are available.

President Droupadi Murmu on January 26, 2026 conferred India's highest peacetime gallantry award, Ashoka Chakra, to Group Captain [1],
who created history by becoming the first Indian to set foot on the International Space Station (ISS). The President presented the award to
[1] at the Republic Day celebrations at the Kartavya Path, the centrepiece boulevard of the national capital. In June last year, [1] became the
second Indian to have gone to space and the first to visit the ISS as part of the historic Axiom-4 mission. His 18-day space odyssey came
41 years after cosmonaut Rakesh Sharma flew aboard the Russian Soyuz-11 space mission. As a fighter pilot, [1] has an impressive
record of 2,000 hours of flight experience across various aircraft, including the Su-30 MKI, MiG-21, MiG-29, Jaguar, Hawk, Dornier, and An-
32, [1] served as pilot for the Axiom Mission 4 (Ax-4) to the International Space Station and left an indelible mark on India's remarkable
advancements in human space exploration. After the successful space mission, Group Captain [1] became a household name as his
contribution during the mission, including the conduct of sophisticated experiments, received recognition from global space experts. The
Axiom-4 mission was executed by US-based private firm Axiom Space, and it involved NASA, European Space Agency (Esa) and the Indian
Space Research Organisation (ISRO). Group Captain [1] hails from Lucknow. He was commissioned into the fighter stream of the Indian
Air Force in June 2006.

India's Manu Bhaker had to settle for a silver medal in the women's 25 m pistol event at the ongoing Asian Shooting Championships 2026
in New Delhi on Monday after losing in a shootoff. In the eight-woman shootout, Manu Bhaker, who won two medals at the Paris 2024
Olympics, began slowly but mounted a late surge to draw level with Vietnam's Nguyen Thuy Trang at 35-35 after the regulation 50 shots,
fired in 10 series of five. The Indian shooter was earlier trailing Trang by three shots after the fourth series. However, Manu Bhaker failed to
follow up in the tie-breaking shootoff. After finishing the first round at 2-2, Trang clinched the second one 3-2 to win the gold. Incidentally,
this was Manu Bhaker's first-ever individual continental shooting medal in the 25m pistol. Her previous three, including two golds, were all
in the 10m air pistol. Manu Bhaker endured a disappointing outing at this year's 10m air pistol event as she finished seventh in the
individual category. However, she helped India clinch gold in the team category of the event. In the 10 m air pistol mixed team event, Manu
Bhaker failed to make the final. Meanwhile, Olympian Esha Singh, who became the 10m air pistol women's Asian champion earlier in the
competition, bagged the bronze medal in the 25m event on Sunday with a score of 30.

options: She became the first Indian shooter to win Olympic gold.
She became the first Indian woman to compete in shooting.
She became the first Indian athlete to win multiple medals at a single Olympics.
She became the youngest Olympic medalist from India.

Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required
to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.

Passage – 1


In a recent judgment, the Supreme Court examined whether a surviving participant in a suicide pact may be held liable for abetment of
suicide under Sections 306 and 107 of the Indian Penal Code. The case arose from the death of a young actress who consumed
organophosphate pesticide alongside her partner following opposition to their relationship. While she died, the accused survived and was
convicted of abetment.


The Court clarified that abetment under Section 107 IPC is not confined to physically supplying the means of suicide. It includes
instigation, intentional aid, and participation that provides psychological reinforcement directly connected to the commission of suicide. In
a suicide pact, the Court observed, there exists a "reciprocal commitment": each participant's resolve to die is strengthened and sustained
by the other's active participation. The act becomes conditional upon mutual involvement, since withdrawal by one may deter the other.


The Court reasoned that such mutual reinforcement supplies the necessary "impetus" for the act. The State's fundamental interest in
preserving life justifies criminalising conduct that intentionally supports or facilitates self-destruction. A shared decision to die does not
dilute criminal liability; rather, it may strengthen the inference of intentional aid where both parties actively participate.


However, the Court drew distinctions. Mere presence at the scene, passive knowledge of suicidal intent, or harassment unconnected to
the suicide would not automatically amount to abetment. Liability requires intentional conduct that directly facilitates, strengthens, or
sustains the deceased's decision to commit suicide.


In the case before it, the accused had purchased the pesticide, consumed it alongside the deceased, and did not claim coercion or
domination. His conduct demonstrated reciprocal commitment and active participation.


The Court therefore held that entering into and acting upon a suicide pact may attract liability under Section 107 IPC where psychological
reinforcement and intentional participation are established.

to die, neither can be said to have aided or instigated the other. Applying the passage, which conclusion is most legally sustainable?
options: B cannot be liable because independent suicidal intent of both parties breaks the chain of instigation.
B's liability depends exclusively on whether he supplied the poison
B cannot be liable unless it is proven that A would not have committed suicide without B's presence.

B may be liable because mutual agreement combined with simultaneous participation may amount to intentional psychological
reinforcement sufficient for abetment.

Passage – 2


In a recent decision, the Supreme Court acquitted a man convicted of murdering his six-year-old stepdaughter, holding that a disclosure
statement leading to discovery of material evidence is admissible under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act only if the accused was in
police custody at the time the statement was made.


Section 27 permits proof of so much of the information received from an accused in custody as distinctly relates to the fact thereby
discovered. The Court clarified that custody does not necessarily mean formal arrest; it may include surveillance or restraint sufficient to
curtail freedom. However, in the present case, the memorandum recording the disclosure was prepared at 10:30 a.m., while the arrest
memo showed formal arrest at 10:00 p.m. the same day. There was no evidence of restraint, surveillance, or restriction on liberty when the
statement was recorded. The disclosure therefore fell outside Section 27.


Relying on precedent, the Court reiterated that if the accused was not in custody when the statement was made, discovery evidence
cannot be admitted under Section 27. However, such conduct may still be admissible under Section 8 of the Evidence Act as relevant
conduct. The Court emphasised that Section 8 evidence is weak and can only corroborate other strong evidence; it cannot independently
sustain conviction.


The Court also observed that while DNA confirmed the child's death, it did not conclusively connect the accused to the crime. There was a
long unexplained delay in reporting the child missing, despite the family knowing she was last seen with the accused. Further, the corpus
delicti was not fully recovered, and no precise time of death could be established.


Granting benefit of doubt, the Court acquitted the accused. The ruling reinforces that evidentiary safeguards including the custody

requirement under Section 27 and the protection against compelled self-incrimination under Article 20(3) must be strictly observed,
particularly where conviction rests on circumstantial evidence.
content.questionText:
Police informally question X at his home regarding a missing child. During the interaction, without any formal arrest or restraint, X
reveals the location of skeletal remains, which are subsequently recovered. Later that evening, he is formally arrested. The prosecution
seeks to rely on the disclosure under Section 27. Based on the passage, which is the most legally sustainable conclusion?
options: The disclosure is inadmissible under Section 27 because X was not in police custody at the time of making the statement.
The disclosure is admissible because recovery of remains conclusively establishes reliability.
The disclosure is admissible since formal arrest later validates prior statements.
The disclosure is admissible under Section 27 but automatically inadmissible for all other purposes.

In a recent decision, the Supreme Court revisited the delicate balance between consumer rights and evidentiary discipline in awarding
compensation. The case concerned a model who claimed that a faulty haircut at a luxury hotel salon caused professional setbacks and
emotional trauma, seeking damages exceeding Rs.5 crores.


The National Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission (NCDRC) had awarded Rs.2 crores as compensation, relying primarily on
photocopies of documents produced by the complainant.


The Supreme Court set aside the award, reiterating that while consumer protection law seeks to provide effective remedies against
deficiency in service, compensation must be grounded in credible and reliable evidence. The Court emphasized that damages-especially
of substantial magnitude-cannot be awarded based on presumptions, sympathy, or general discussion of loss. Where claims run into
crores of rupees, the complainant must establish actual loss through trustworthy material.


The Court observed that merely producing photocopies of documents, without adequate authentication or corroboration, is insufficient to
justify large-scale compensation. It rejected the reasoning that trauma or emotional distress could justify relaxation of evidentiary
standards in quantifying damages. Even if original documents are unavailable, the claimant must adopt appropriate legal means to
substantiate claims.


Notably, the Court did not deny that deficiency in service may entitle a consumer to compensation. However, it clarified that the quantum
must bear rational connection to proven loss. Consumer fora are not free to award excessive damages on a "thumb rule" basis when the
stakes involve crores of rupees.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required
to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 4


Vicarious liability is a doctrine under tort law whereby one person is held liable for the wrongful acts of another, not because of personal
fault, but because of the legal relationship between them. Most commonly, it arises in the employer-employee relationship. The rationale
lies in the employer's control over the employee's work and the benefit derived from the enterprise.


For vicarious liability to arise, two conditions must ordinarily be satisfied: first, the existence of a relationship akin to employment; and
second, the wrongful act must have been committed in the course of employment.


The expression "in the course of employment" does not require that the act be authorised. Even unauthorised or wrongful modes of
performing authorised acts may attract liability, provided there is sufficient connection between the employee's duties and the wrongful
act.

However, if the employee embarks on a "frolic of his own" - that is, acts wholly outside the scope of employment for personal purposes -
the employer is not liable. The distinction lies in whether the wrongful act is closely connected to the tasks the employee was engaged to
perform.


The doctrine also extends in certain circumstances beyond traditional contracts of service. Courts examine factors such as control,
integration into the business, and economic dependence to determine whether the relationship is sufficiently akin to employment.
Independent contractors, in general, do not impose vicarious liability on those who engage them, unless the activity involves non-delegable
duties or inherently hazardous operations.


Ultimately, the principle balances fairness and risk distribution: since employers profit from enterprise activities and have the ability to
regulate risks, they may bear responsibility for harms arising from acts sufficiently connected to those activities. However, liability does
not arise merely because a relationship exists; the connection between the wrongful act and employment remains the decisive inquiry.

making deliveries. However, R had taken a minor detour of two streets to buy coffee before continuing the assigned route. The
pedestrian sues the company. Applying the passage, which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The company is liable because R was still engaged in the employer's business despite a minor deviation.
The company is not liable because any deviation from assigned route automatically constitutes a frolic.
The company is not liable because purchasing coffee is a personal act unrelated to employment.
The company is liable only if the detour was expressly authorised.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required
to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 5


Under contract law, consent is free only when not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, or misrepresentation. Fraud involves a false
representation made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly, with intent to deceive another party and induce them into a
contract. Misrepresentation, in contrast, involves an untrue statement of fact made innocently or negligently, without intent to deceive, but
which nonetheless induces the contract.


The essential distinction lies in the representor's state of mind. Fraud requires intention to deceive; misrepresentation does not. However,
both render the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party if the statement materially induced consent.


Silence does not ordinarily amount to fraud. A party is generally under no duty to disclose material facts, as contracts are based on caveat
emptor (buyer beware). However, silence may amount to fraud where there exists a duty to speak - such as in fiduciary relationships,
contracts of utmost good faith, or where silence is equivalent to speech. Likewise, active concealment of a fact is fraud, even if no express
false statement is made.


A mere statement of opinion, puffery, or future intention is not actionable unless it implies a false assertion of fact or the maker never
intended to perform it at the time of making the statement. The law distinguishes between false promises (made without intention to
perform) and mere breach of contract.


Importantly, if the aggrieved party had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence and failed to do so, relief for
misrepresentation may be denied. However, this defence is weaker in cases of fraud, as the law does not expect a party to investigate
deliberate deceit.


Thus, the doctrines of fraud and misrepresentation balance commercial certainty with fairness: not every inaccurate statement voids a
contract, but deception that vitiates consent cannot be tolerated.

A sells land to B stating that "the soil is highly fertile." A honestly believes this to be true based on local reputation but has never
personally tested the soil. It later turns out that the soil quality is poor. B seeks to rescind the contract. Which is the most legally
sustainable conclusion under the passage?
options: The statement amounts to fraud because A made an unverified factual claim inducing the contract.
The contract cannot be rescinded because B could have independently tested the soil.
The statement is neither fraud nor misrepresentation because soil fertility is always a matter of opinion.

The statement may amount to misrepresentation if it was presented as fact and materially induced B's consent, despite absence of
intent to deceive.

Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required
to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 5


Under contract law, consent is free only when not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, or misrepresentation. Fraud involves a false
representation made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly, with intent to deceive another party and induce them into a
contract. Misrepresentation, in contrast, involves an untrue statement of fact made innocently or negligently, without intent to deceive, but
which nonetheless induces the contract.


The essential distinction lies in the representor's state of mind. Fraud requires intention to deceive; misrepresentation does not. However,
both render the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party if the statement materially induced consent.


Silence does not ordinarily amount to fraud. A party is generally under no duty to disclose material facts, as contracts are based on caveat
emptor (buyer beware). However, silence may amount to fraud where there exists a duty to speak - such as in fiduciary relationships,
contracts of utmost good faith, or where silence is equivalent to speech. Likewise, active concealment of a fact is fraud, even if no express
false statement is made.


A mere statement of opinion, puffery, or future intention is not actionable unless it implies a false assertion of fact or the maker never
intended to perform it at the time of making the statement. The law distinguishes between false promises (made without intention to
perform) and mere breach of contract.


Importantly, if the aggrieved party had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence and failed to do so, relief for
misrepresentation may be denied. However, this defence is weaker in cases of fraud, as the law does not expect a party to investigate
deliberate deceit.


Thus, the doctrines of fraud and misrepresentation balance commercial certainty with fairness: not every inaccurate statement voids a
contract, but deception that vitiates consent cannot be tolerated.

fiduciary relationship between F and G, and G never inquires about pending issues. Which conclusion is most aligned with the passage?
options: Silence amounts to fraud because the information was material.
Silence amounts to misrepresentation because non-disclosure induced consent.
Silence does not amount to fraud unless there was a duty to disclose or active concealment.
Silence automatically renders the contract voidable.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required
to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 6


Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code embodies the principle of joint liability based on common intention. It does not create a separate
offence but attributes liability to each participant when a criminal act is done in furtherance of a shared design. The essence of Section 34
lies in the existence of a prior meeting of minds and participation in the act pursuant to that shared intention. The meeting of minds need
not be premeditated long in advance; it may develop on the spot. However, it must be evidenced by coordinated conduct reflecting unity of
purpose.

Participation need not always involve inflicting the fatal blow; even minimal but conscious involvement that facilitates the execution of the
shared plan may suffice. Mere presence at the scene, however, even with knowledge of the offence, does not automatically attract liability
unless it indicates active alignment with the criminal design.


The distinction between common intention and similar intention is crucial. Similar intention refers to independent but coinciding intentions
without prior concert. In such cases, each person is liable only for his own act.


Liability under Section 34 extends to acts done within the scope of the shared design or those that are probable and foreseeable
consequences of that design. However, if one participant commits an act fundamentally different from what was contemplated, and
others neither knew nor adopted the expanded intention, joint liability may not attach.


Thus, the requirements of Section 34 are:
(i) a meeting of minds (which may arise suddenly),
(ii) participation in furtherance of that intention, and
(iii) the act committed being within the scope of, or a foreseeable extension of, the shared design.


Inference must be drawn from conduct, coordination, and surrounding circumstances and not mere association.
content.questionText:
A, B, and C agree to assault D with sticks after a verbal altercation. During the assault, A unexpectedly pulls out a concealed
firearm and fatally shoots D. There is no evidence that B and C were aware of the firearm or that firearms were discussed. Which
conclusion best accords with the passage?
options: B and C are liable for murder because they participated in the assault which resulted in death.
B and C are liable because once common intention to assault exists, liability extends to all consequences.
B and C are not liable because they did not personally fire the gun.
B and C are liable only if the shooting was within the scope of the shared design or a foreseeable extension of it.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 83 to 108: Read the passages and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


In a quiet township, a close group of friends lived in separate houses arranged neatly along streets that ran strictly north–south and east–
west. To make giving directions more interesting, they created a symbolic code to describe the location of each other's houses. Instead of
using lengthy descriptions, they combined symbols with numbers. For example, A 50@ B meant that A's house was 50 metres north of B's
house, while C 30# D indicated that C's house was 30 metres east of D's house. Similarly, the symbols $ and & were used to represent
south and west respectively, each accompanied by the exact distance.


Eight friends P, Q, R, S, T, U, V, and W would challenge each other to decode who lived where, calculate distances, and figure out relative
positions - all using these symbols. Over time, the town's simple map transformed into a puzzle of symbols, numbers, and logic, making
everyday directions an engaging exercise in reasoning and spatial thinking. It is also known that:


P 600@ Q ; Q 800# R ; R 1000$ S ; S 400& T ; T 600@ U
content.questionText: In which direction is P's house with respect to S's house?
options: North-East
North-West
South-East
South-West

Passage – 2


Rohan Verma has applied to the Master's programme in Data Science at the National Institute for Data and Society Studies. The institute
is known for academic rigor and social responsibility.


Admission Guidelines
Applicants must:
• secure at least 60% in graduation
• have studied Mathematics at Class XII or graduation level
• submit a valid entrance test score from the past two years


The institute also states:
• admissions are holistic, considering innovation, work, and social impact
• it values equity and inclusion, especially for disadvantaged applicants
• in borderline cases, discretion may be used for resilience and contribution


Rohan's Situation
• Graduation marks: 58%
• Final-year exams affected by hospitalization
• Mathematics studied at Class XII

• Valid entrance test score
• Volunteered teaching data literacy in rural schools for three years
• Built a mobile app delivering weather alerts to small farmers
• First-generation college student from a low-income household


Rohan learns that his marks fall short of eligibility. He must decide how to present his case and respond to possible objections while
maintaining honesty and self-respect.
content.questionText:
Rohan is unsure whether to submit an additional note explaining his illness and academic shortfall. Which of the following would
be a correct course of action?
options: Provide a truthful explanation with medical documentation to clarify the context of his academic record.
Avoid mentioning the illness so that the committee evaluates him without perceiving weakness or vulnerability.
Emphasize the illness dramatically to increase sympathy and improve the chances of favorable consideration.
Focus only on achievements since eligibility rules rarely permit contextual exceptions to academic thresholds.

On the evening of March 3rd, the historic Sapphire Seal disappeared from a locked display case inside the Heritage Hall of the State
Archives. The theft occurred sometime between the hall's closing at 8:00 PM and the security supervisor's inspection at 11:30 PM, when
the case was discovered empty.


Three former employees - recently dismissed after an internal audit - were considered suspects:
Devika, the former archivist
Karan, the former security technician
Leela, the former exhibition stylist


Established Facts
• The display case could only be opened using a six-digit override code known exclusively to Devika and the archives director (who was
attending a conference abroad).
• Karan claimed he was attending a film screening from 7:30 PM to 11:45 PM. Ticket scans and CCTV confirm he remained inside the
cinema the entire time.
• Leela stated she was working at a printing press across town. Entry logs show her entering at 6:45 PM and exiting at 10:40 PM. The
press is 30 minutes away from the archives.
• The security supervisor confirmed that during a routine round at 9:00 PM, the Sapphire Seal was still in the case.
• Investigators recovered a distinctive teal fabric thread caught in the display case hinge. Devika owns a shawl made from rare teal silk of a

similar weave.
• Karan had previously claimed he could bypass magnetic locking systems remotely, including the model installed on the display case.
However, system logs show the case was opened via correct code entry.
content.questionText:
Identifying the Most Likely Suspect
Based only on the fact that the override code was used, who is the only plausible suspect?
options: Devika
Karan
Leela
Devika and Leela

Prime Mock CLAT - 5 2027
Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


When a five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India delivered its verdict, in September 2018, in Indian Young Lawyers Association vs
State of Kerala, opening the doors of Kerala's Sabarimala temple to women of all ages, it provoked a range of reactions. There were
protests across the country, especially in Kerala, where many believed that the Court had overlooked, and even disrespected, religious
creed. Others saw the verdict as transformative, as outlining a vision that enlivened the Constitution. Now, close to a decade later, the
Court will hear final arguments on review petitions that seek to overturn the earlier verdict and the law it laid down.


The original ruling was delivered through a 4:1 majority. There was an opinion from then Chief Justice of India (CJI) Dipak Misra, to which
Justice A.M. Khanwilkar joined, and separate concurring opinions from Justices Rohinton Nariman and D.Y. Chandrachud, and a notable
dissent from Justice Indu Malhotra.


The majority's findings were clear. First, the Court ruled that the devotees of Lord Ayyappa did not constitute a separate religious
denomination; second, that the bar enforced on women between the ages of 10 and 50 from entering the temple violated the rights of
women to freedom of religion; and third, that Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965,
on which the ban was grounded, violated not only the Constitution but also Section 3 of its parent law, which promised free access to
temples for all classes of Hindus.


In her dissenting opinion, Justice Malhotra found that a generic doctrine of equality cannot override the collective rights of individuals to
practise their faith in line with their customs and ideals. She also found that, as a matter of custom, women of a certain age had been
excluded from the temple's precincts, and this constituted a non-derogable "essential religious practice."


The latter finding represented the central axis on which the case turned. The Constitution recognises both the freedom of religion as an
individual right and the rights of religious denominations to manage their own affairs in matters of religion. Both rights are subject to
public order, morality and health.


Balancing communitarian interests with individual conscience has long plagued our jurisprudence. Over the years, when it has been called
to resolve tensions of this kind, the Court has used a test that has allowed it to virtually sit in theological judgment over religious practice.
That is, it examines and arrives at a factual conclusion on whether a practice in question is essential to the religion or not. This has meant
that the Court has effectively determined not only those areas where it might be constitutionally justifiable for the state to intervene but
has also determined what kinds of practices are deserving of constitutional protection in the first place.


( 468 words, Source: Hindu Editorial)
content.questionText: The main idea of the passage is:
options: The Sabarimala review's final arguments will centre on the age-old traditions of a particular temple.
The Supreme Court has not quite managed to balance faith and constitutional rights.
The Sabarimala review involves the broader architecture of India's religious freedom jurisprudence.
The Sabarimala review favours constitutional rights and individual dignity over faith and tradition.

Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


When a five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India delivered its verdict, in September 2018, in Indian Young Lawyers Association vs
State of Kerala, opening the doors of Kerala's Sabarimala temple to women of all ages, it provoked a range of reactions. There were
protests across the country, especially in Kerala, where many believed that the Court had overlooked, and even disrespected, religious
creed. Others saw the verdict as transformative, as outlining a vision that enlivened the Constitution. Now, close to a decade later, the
Court will hear final arguments on review petitions that seek to overturn the earlier verdict and the law it laid down.


The original ruling was delivered through a 4:1 majority. There was an opinion from then Chief Justice of India (CJI) Dipak Misra, to which
Justice A.M. Khanwilkar joined, and separate concurring opinions from Justices Rohinton Nariman and D.Y. Chandrachud, and a notable
dissent from Justice Indu Malhotra.


The majority's findings were clear. First, the Court ruled that the devotees of Lord Ayyappa did not constitute a separate religious
denomination; second, that the bar enforced on women between the ages of 10 and 50 from entering the temple violated the rights of
women to freedom of religion; and third, that Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965,
on which the ban was grounded, violated not only the Constitution but also Section 3 of its parent law, which promised free access to
temples for all classes of Hindus.


In her dissenting opinion, Justice Malhotra found that a generic doctrine of equality cannot override the collective rights of individuals to
practise their faith in line with their customs and ideals. She also found that, as a matter of custom, women of a certain age had been
excluded from the temple's precincts, and this constituted a non-derogable "essential religious practice."


The latter finding represented the central axis on which the case turned. The Constitution recognises both the freedom of religion as an
individual right and the rights of religious denominations to manage their own affairs in matters of religion. Both rights are subject to
public order, morality and health.


Balancing communitarian interests with individual conscience has long plagued our jurisprudence. Over the years, when it has been called
to resolve tensions of this kind, the Court has used a test that has allowed it to virtually sit in theological judgment over religious practice.
That is, it examines and arrives at a factual conclusion on whether a practice in question is essential to the religion or not. This has meant
that the Court has effectively determined not only those areas where it might be constitutionally justifiable for the state to intervene but
has also determined what kinds of practices are deserving of constitutional protection in the first place.


( 468 words, Source: Hindu Editorial)

options: The Supreme Court is fully justified in determining religious practices.
The essential religious practice test is inherently flawed.
The Court has fulfilled its role as gatekeeper but failed as arbiter.
Judicial intervention in religious matters is necessary for legitimising the Court's authority.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2


These archaic humans loved, played, formed close friendships, and competed for status and power - but so did chimps, baboons and
elephants. There was nothing special about humans. Nobody, least of all humans themselves, had any inkling that their descendants
would one day walk on the moon, split the atom, fathom the genetic code, and write history books. The most important thing to know
about prehistoric humans is that they were insignificant animals with no more impact on their environment than gorillas, fireflies, or
jellyfish.

Just 6 million years ago, a single female ape had two daughters. One became the ancestor of all chimps, the other is our own
grandmother. Humans first evolved in East Africa about 2.5 million years ago from an earlier genus of apes called Australopithecus. About
2 million years ago, some of these archaic people left their homeland to settle vast areas of North Africa, Europe, and Asia. Since survival
in the snowy forests of northern Europe required different traits than those needed in Indonesia's steaming jungles, human populations
evolved in different directions, producing several distinct species.


Despite their differences, all human species share several defining characteristics. Most notably, humans have extraordinarily large brains.
Modern Sapiens sport a brain averaging 73-85 cubic inches, consuming 25% of the body's energy at rest - compared to only 8% in other
apes. Archaic humans paid for their large brains in two ways: they spent more time searching for food, and their muscles atrophied. Like a
government diverting money from defence to education, humans diverted energy from biceps to neurons. A chimp cannot win an
argument with a Homo sapiens, but the ape can rip the man apart like a ragdoll.


Yet for more than 2 million years, despite big brains and sharp stone tools, humans remained weak and marginal creatures - dwelling in
constant fear of predators, rarely hunting large game, and subsisting mainly by gathering plants and eating carrion left behind by more
powerful carnivores. One of the most common uses of stone tools was to crack open bones to extract marrow - a humble niche not unlike
that of a woodpecker extracting insects from tree trunks.


It is a common fallacy to envision human species as arranged in a straight line of descent. The truth is that from about 2 million years ago
until around 10,000 years ago, the world was simultaneously home to several human species. It is our current exclusivity, not that multi-
species past, that is peculiar - and perhaps incriminating.


(412 words, Source: Sapiens)
content.questionText:
What does the author imply by stating that prehistoric humans had "no more impact on their environment than gorillas, fireflies or
jellyfish"?
options: prehistoric humans were closer in their genetic makeup to gorillas and fireflies than to modern humans.
the ecology was in an inchoate state, so prehistoric humans could not have any adverse impact on it.
prehistoric humans, gorillas, fireflies and jellyfish occupied identical positions in the animal kingdom.
human exceptionalism was not a given - it was an emergence, not a starting condition.

Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 3


Eileen Gu is the most decorated freestyle skier in the history of the Olympics. She is tough, bright, and fearless. She is also, it turns out, a
journaller. In a recent press interaction, the 22-year-old responded to a query about her ability to respond thoughtfully to questions on any
subject from "geopolitics to sports to aerodynamics", by talking about the writing habit that helps her "break down her thought processes".


Because thinking is an activity that requires far more intention than merely allowing thoughts to drift in. Left alone, an idea or impression
may well float out again and be lost forever. Writing is what makes the nebulous concrete; by forcing the brain to pay attention, it forces
the assembling and synthesising of information, pinning down the elusive and making connections that illuminate and define.


There is evidence to back up the assertion that writing clarifies thought and shapes understanding and perception. Multiple studies have
shown a strong link between the physical act of writing and the creation and deepening of interconnections in the brain's vast neural
network, leading to better memory and comprehension.


Writers, of course, have always known this: To write is to think. Indeed, Joan Didion once said that she never really knows what she is
thinking until she has put pen to paper - a conviction echoed by other practitioners of the written word, such as Flannery O'Connor,
Stephen King and Kurt Vonnegut. In the age of the intelligent machine, it is good to remember that it is these small acts of rigour - of
observation, record and clarification - that really shape human knowledge.


(266 words, Editorial, The Indian express)

Thinking is an intentional, more passive process, whereas writing is an active, disciplined one.
Most people think clearly enough without writing, but writers require it as a professional habit.
The act of writing and the act of thinking are essentially the same cognitive process.

Eileen Gu is the most decorated freestyle skier in the history of the Olympics. She is tough, bright, and fearless. She is also, it turns out, a

subject from "geopolitics to sports to aerodynamics", by talking about the writing habit that helps her "break down her thought processes".


Because thinking is an activity that requires far more intention than merely allowing thoughts to drift in. Left alone, an idea or impression
may well float out again and be lost forever. Writing is what makes the nebulous concrete; by forcing the brain to pay attention, it forces
the assembling and synthesising of information, pinning down the elusive and making connections that illuminate and define.


There is evidence to back up the assertion that writing clarifies thought and shapes understanding and perception. Multiple studies have
shown a strong link between the physical act of writing and the creation and deepening of interconnections in the brain's vast neural
network, leading to better memory and comprehension.

thinking until she has put pen to paper - a conviction echoed by other practitioners of the written word, such as Flannery O'Connor,
Stephen King and Kurt Vonnegut. In the age of the intelligent machine, it is good to remember that it is these small acts of rigour - of
observation, record and clarification - that really shape human knowledge.

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 1 to 24: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 4


A public interest petition before the Supreme Court has challenged expansive search and seizure powers granted to Income Tax
authorities under the Income Tax Act, 2025, which authorise access to "computer systems" and "virtual digital space", including personal
electronic devices, cloud servers and private electronic communications. The challenge is directed at provisions that permit searches
based on an officer's belief that a person "will not" or "would not" produce documents if summoned, or that assets "would not be
disclosed" for tax purposes. According to the petitioner, these clauses create an "anticipatory" search framework, enabling intrusive action
even in the absence of any existing violation of law.


Hegde acknowledged that Section 132 of the 1961 Act had been upheld by the Supreme Court in Pooran Mal v Director of Inspection
(1974), but argued that the ruling must be revisited in light of the recognition of the right to privacy as a fundamental right in K S
Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017). He submitted that the Income Tax Act provides no effective safeguards, particularly since the
"reasons to believe" justifying a search need not be disclosed and are insulated from scrutiny even before appellate tribunals following a
2017 amendment.


Justice Bagchi, however, noted that the Supreme Court had recognised a limited scope of judicial review over the exercise of search
powers under Section 132 in its 2022 decision in Principal Director of Income Tax (Investigation) v Laljibhai Kanjibhai Mandalia. He
observed that courts can call for departmental records and examine whether a rational nexus exists between the material available with
tax authorities and the belief recorded for initiating a search.


CJI Surya Kant observed that in cases involving electronic evidence, individuals could destroy the device itself. Justice Bagchi added that
much digital evidence, particularly social media data, historically resided in the cloud or on foreign servers, limiting investigative access.
Destroying devices, he noted, could effectively derail investigations.


Hegde countered that technological methods exist for data recovery but maintained that the law must prescribe clear safeguards to
prevent abuse. The Chief Justice said the provision was not an "uncontrolled power" and operated subject to statutory preconditions. "At
present, there is only an apprehension. Let us see how the law is implemented over time," he said.


The plea contends that this expansion of search powers into the digital domain constitutes a serious invasion of informational privacy
under Article 21. It further argues that existing statutory tools such as summons, surveys and assessments are less intrusive alternatives,
and that permitting full-scale digital searches on speculative grounds fails the constitutional test of proportionality.


The petitioner has sought a declaration striking down the challenged provisions, or a reading down of the law with safeguards such as
independent oversight, disclosure of reasons and guidelines to prevent misuse of digital search powers.
content.questionText: Which of the following best describes the central constitutional challenge raised in the petition?
options: That the Income Tax Act, 2025 was passed without adequate parliamentary debate on digital privacy concerns.
That anticipatory digital search powers under the Income Tax Act violate informational privacy guaranteed under Article 21.
That Income Tax authorities currently lack the technical expertise to handle digital evidence in a responsible manner.
That cloud servers and foreign data repositories should be fully exempt from all domestic tax investigations.

Directions for questions 25 to 52: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


The assassination of Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was the culmination of decades of painstaking intelligence gathering
by Israeli secret services, with crucial technological resources and manpower provided over the last six months by the CIA and other US
intelligence services, which culminated in a single concentrated burst of lethal violence to decapitate the Iranian regime, according to
experts, veteran spies and officials in Israel and the US. Khamenei was killed along with seven "members of the top Iranian security
leadership who had gathered at several locations in Tehran" and about a dozen members of his family and close entourage in near-

simultaneous strikes within 60 seconds, military officials in Israel said. Forty other senior Iranian leaders also died in the attack.


The killing of Khamenei, 86, opened the air offensive launched this weekend by Israel and the US in an effort to overthrow the radical
clerical regime in Tehran, plunging the Middle East into renewed chaos and violence. Some experts and intelligence veterans, however,
described a possible strategic error that could alienate potential supporters or open the way for more radical opponents in the future. "The
problem is that Israel is in love with assassinations … and we never learn that it is not the solution. We have killed all the leaders of Hamas.
They are still there. It's the same with Hezbollah. The leaders are always replaced," said Yossi Melman, a respected Israeli analyst and
author specialising in intelligence. Israel has a long history of conducting assassinations overseas, but has never before killed a head of
state.
content.questionText: Ali Hosseini Khamenei was associated with which major historical event in Iran?
options: The Iranian Revolution
The Constitutional Revolution
The Green Movement
The Arab Spring

Directions for questions 25 to 52: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2


The Winter Olympics ended as the twin flames in host cities Milan and Cortina d'Ampezzo were extinguished during a closing ceremony at
the ancient Verona Arena, roughly mid-distance between the far-flung mountain, valley and city venues that made these the most spread-
out Winter Games ever. In declaring the 2026 Games over, International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry told local organisers
that they "delivered a new kind of Winter Games and you set a new, very high standard for the future". The next Winter Games will be held
in neighbouring France, which received the Olympic flag in the official handover earlier in the ceremony. Following the same spread-out
model, the 2030 Winter Games will stage events in the Alps and Nice, on the Mediterranean Sea, while speed skating will be held either in
Italy or the Netherlands.


A total of 116 medal events were held in eight Olympic sports across 16 disciplines, including the debut of ski mountaineering this year,
over the course of 17 days of competition. With the final events wrapping up just hours before the ceremony, the 50km mass start men's
and women's cross-country medals were awarded by Coventry inside the arena. Hosts Italy won their highest Winter Olympic tally of 30
medals, including 10 gold and six silver, surpassing the previous record of 20 medals, set at the Lillehammer Olympics in 1994. The
closing ceremony paid tribute to Italian dance and music, from lyric opera to Italian pop of the 20th century to the DJ beat of Gabry Ponte,
who got the 1,500 athletes on their feet and dancing while colourful confetti exploded on stage. Italian artist Achille Lauro delivered the
last word with the song "Incoscienti Giovani", or "reckless young people", just before athletes who had so aptly harnessed their youthful
energy for these games filed out.

options: Tina and Milo
Neve and Gliz
Bing Dwen Dwen and Shuey Rhon Rhon
Wenlock and Mandeville

content.passageText:
Directions for questions 25 to 52: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 3


The Supreme Court, in an order, upheld the inclusion of 'socialist, secular' in the Preamble of the Constitution. "The word 'secular' denotes
a Republic that upholds equal respect for all religions. 'Socialist' represents a Republic dedicated to eliminating all forms of exploitation -
whether social, political, or economic," a Bench of Chief Justice of India Sanjiv Khanna and Justice Sanjay Kumar interpreted. The order
was based on a batch of petitions filed in 2020 challenging the validity of the inclusion of 'socialist' and 'secular' in the Preamble through
the [1] Constitution Amendment in 1976. The petitioners, who included Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Subramanian Swamy, argued
that the insertions made with retrospective effect, that is, from the date of adoption of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly on
November 26, 1949 amounted to a fraud on the Constitution. Besides, they argued, the word 'secular' was deliberately eschewed by the
Constituent Assembly and the word 'socialist' fettered the economic policy choice of the elected government, which represents the will of
the people.


The apex court said, in its seven-page order, that the case was not worth a detailed adjudication as the flaws in the petitioners' arguments
were manifest. Moreover, the court found the motives of the petitions, filed nearly 44 years after 'secular' and 'socialist' were inserted in the
Preamble, "questionable". The court held that the Preamble was an inalienable part of the Constitution. The Parliament had an
unquestionable power to amend the Constitution under Article 368. Its power to amend extended to the Preamble. The court confirmed
the retrospective amendment to the Preamble, saying the date of adoption would not curtail the power under Article [2]. The court
explained that the Constitution was a "living document", and open to changes according to the needs of the time. Though the Constituent
Assembly was not sure about what 'secularism' should entail in India, the court said, over time the nation has developed its own
interpretation of the term, which has become a basic feature of the Constitution.


"Over time, India has developed its own interpretation of secularism, wherein the State neither supports any religion nor penalises the
profession and practice of any faith. This principle is enshrined in Articles 14, 15, and 16 of the Constitution, which prohibit discrimination

against citizens on religious grounds while guaranteeing equal protection of laws and equal opportunity in public employment," the
Supreme Court observed. The apex court clarified that 'socialism' in the Indian context meant the commitment to function as a welfare
state. "Neither the Constitution nor the Preamble mandates a specific economic policy or structure, whether left or right. Rather, 'socialist'
denotes the state's commitment to be a welfare state and its commitment to ensuring equality of opportunity. India has consistently
embraced a mixed economy model, where the private sector has flourished, expanded, and grown over the years," the apex court
highlighted.
content.questionText:
The words "socialist" and "secular" were inserted into the Preamble by which Constitutional Amendment act redacted with [1] in
the passage above?
options: 44th Constitutional Amendment
42nd Constitutional Amendment
39th Constitutional Amendment
33rd Constitutional Amendment

the award was "unanimous", said Doyle. Joining him on this year's panel was the actor Sarah Jessica Parker, along with the writers Chris
Power, Ayobami Adebayo and Kiley Reid.

Directions for questions 53 to 82: You have been given some passages followed by questions based on each passage. You are required
to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 1


In P. Somaraju v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2025), the Supreme Court reaffirmed a settled principle under the Prevention of Corruption Act,
1988 (PC Act) - that mere recovery of tainted currency notes is insufficient for conviction unless the prosecution establishes both demand
and voluntary acceptance of illegal gratification beyond reasonable doubt. The Court, through a Bench comprising Justices P.K. Mishra
and Joymalya Bagchi, set aside the Andhra Pradesh High Court's order convicting a former Assistant Labour Commissioner, restoring the
trial court's acquittal. The Court noted that the prosecution's case rested solely on the uncorroborated testimony of the complainant, which
was riddled with inconsistencies. The purported independent witness designated by the police to observe the transaction had, contrary to
instructions, remained outside the office during the alleged demand and acceptance, rendering his evidence inconsequential. Rejecting the
High Court's reasoning, the Supreme Court emphasized that the statutory presumption under Section 20 of the PC Act does not arise
automatically. It becomes operative only when the foundational facts of demand and acceptance are proved. The Bench observed that
"without clear proof of the demand and its voluntary acceptance, recovery alone cannot sustain conviction under Sections 7 or 13 of the
Act." The Court also expressed concern over the complainant's conduct in excluding the independent witness from the crucial interaction
period, thereby creating doubt about the fairness of the trap. Although the tainted notes were recovered from the appellant's drawer, there
was no evidence showing that he either demanded or instructed their placement there. Referring to its earlier ruling in Rajesh Gupta v.
State (2022 INSC 359), the Supreme Court concluded that recovery without proof of demand and acceptance is legally inadequate,
acquitted the appellant, and restored the trial court's judgment.


The fight against corruption hinges on the cornerstone: the definition of a 'public servant'. Within the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
(hereinafter referred to as "the PC Act"), this seemingly straightforward term holds immense weight, determining who falls under its
watchful gaze and who remains beyond its reach. However, this line in the sand has shifted and blurred through the tides of time and the
pronouncements of various courts. What constitutes a 'public servant' under the PC Act was comprehensively discussed by the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in Central Bureau of Investigation v. Ramesh Gelli wherein Justice Ranjan Gogoi observed that to ascertain the true
meaning of who is a public servant, the definitions of 'public duty' and 'public servant' have to first be read together closely. Section 2(b) of
the PC Act defines 'public duty' as a duty in the discharge of which the State, the public or the community at large has an interest. Section
2(c)(viii) of the PC Act states that any person who holds an office by virtue of which he is authorised or required to perform any public duty
would be a Public Servant. The first explanation to section 2 provides that persons falling under any of the twelve sub-clauses are public
servants, whether appointed by the Government or not.

options: To limit monetary and non-monetary benefits derived improperly.
The purpose of the act is to limit monetary bribes
The act aims to prevent loss of the government.
The act helps to discipline the government officers.

Passage – 1


In P. Somaraju v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2025), the Supreme Court reaffirmed a settled principle under the Prevention of Corruption Act,
1988 (PC Act) - that mere recovery of tainted currency notes is insufficient for conviction unless the prosecution establishes both demand
and voluntary acceptance of illegal gratification beyond reasonable doubt. The Court, through a Bench comprising Justices P.K. Mishra
and Joymalya Bagchi, set aside the Andhra Pradesh High Court's order convicting a former Assistant Labour Commissioner, restoring the
trial court's acquittal. The Court noted that the prosecution's case rested solely on the uncorroborated testimony of the complainant, which
was riddled with inconsistencies. The purported independent witness designated by the police to observe the transaction had, contrary to
instructions, remained outside the office during the alleged demand and acceptance, rendering his evidence inconsequential. Rejecting the
High Court's reasoning, the Supreme Court emphasized that the statutory presumption under Section 20 of the PC Act does not arise
automatically. It becomes operative only when the foundational facts of demand and acceptance are proved. The Bench observed that
"without clear proof of the demand and its voluntary acceptance, recovery alone cannot sustain conviction under Sections 7 or 13 of the
Act." The Court also expressed concern over the complainant's conduct in excluding the independent witness from the crucial interaction
period, thereby creating doubt about the fairness of the trap. Although the tainted notes were recovered from the appellant's drawer, there
was no evidence showing that he either demanded or instructed their placement there. Referring to its earlier ruling in Rajesh Gupta v.
State (2022 INSC 359), the Supreme Court concluded that recovery without proof of demand and acceptance is legally inadequate,
acquitted the appellant, and restored the trial court's judgment.


The fight against corruption hinges on the cornerstone: the definition of a 'public servant'. Within the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
(hereinafter referred to as "the PC Act"), this seemingly straightforward term holds immense weight, determining who falls under its
watchful gaze and who remains beyond its reach. However, this line in the sand has shifted and blurred through the tides of time and the
pronouncements of various courts. What constitutes a 'public servant' under the PC Act was comprehensively discussed by the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in Central Bureau of Investigation v. Ramesh Gelli wherein Justice Ranjan Gogoi observed that to ascertain the true
meaning of who is a public servant, the definitions of 'public duty' and 'public servant' have to first be read together closely. Section 2(b) of
the PC Act defines 'public duty' as a duty in the discharge of which the State, the public or the community at large has an interest. Section
2(c)(viii) of the PC Act states that any person who holds an office by virtue of which he is authorised or required to perform any public duty
would be a Public Servant. The first explanation to section 2 provides that persons falling under any of the twelve sub-clauses are public
servants, whether appointed by the Government or not.

test. J informed H that he had not prepared for the re-test and requested relaxation on genuine grounds. H stated that promotion was
not possible under the rules but offered to facilitate J's promotion if J paid Rs.50,000. J agreed and was promoted to the next semester.
Can H be held liable for corruption?
options: No, because H is not a public servant.
No, because J voluntarily agreed to pay the money.
Yes, because H demanded illegal gratification in connection with an official act.
No, because H was entitled to charge for granting such favour.

Passage – 2


Trespassing, an act of unauthorized entry onto another's property, stands at the intersection of tort law and criminal law in India. It
encompasses both civil and criminal liabilities, reflecting the need to protect property rights and personal security. Trespassing, in its most
basic form, refers to the unlawful entry onto someone else's property without permission. In the context of tort law, trespassing is an
infringement on the possessory rights of the property owner. The essence of trespassing lies in the unauthorized physical intrusion onto
land, which can be momentary or extended.


Types of Trespass: Trespass to Land: This is the most common form of trespass, involving unauthorized entry onto immovable property.
It includes actions like walking on someone's land, placing objects on it, or causing an object to enter the property.
Trespass to Goods: This involves the wrongful interference with the possessory rights of personal property. Examples include unlawfully
taking or damaging someone's personal belongings.
Trespass to Person: This covers acts of direct physical interference with a person, such as assault, battery, or false imprisonment.


Elements of Trespass to Land
For a successful claim of trespass to land, the plaintiff must establish:
i) Unauthorized Entry: The entry must be without the consent of the property owner or lawful occupier.
ii) Possession of the Property: The plaintiff must have lawful possession of the property at the time of the trespass.
iii) Intention: The entry must be intentional, though intent to cause harm is not necessary. It suffices that the act of entering was deliberate,
even if the trespasser believed they had the right to enter.
iv) Voluntariness: The interference must be voluntary.
v) No Harm Needed
Trespass to land, much like trespass to the person, is a matter of protecting rights, rather than preventing harm. Because of this, no harm
need be shown before a trespass is actionable.
content.questionText: Which of the following is an essential to establish tort of trespass?
options: The property is damaged upon trespass.
Unauthorised access to the property.
An agreement to unlawfully enter upon the land in possession of another.
Taking a license to enter a private property.

A 'bailment' is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is
accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The person delivering the
goods is called the 'bailor'. The person to whom they are delivered is called the 'bailee'. The following are the essential features of
bailment:
(a) Specific Movable Property- A bailer-bailee relation can arise only in case of a specific movable property. There cannot be bailment of
immovable property.
(b) Delivery of Goods for Change of Possession- The essence of bailment is transfer of possession, ownership remaining with the bailor,
change of possession requires delivery of goods.
(c) Delivery for Some Purpose and Usually Upon a Contract- Delivery of goods should be for some purpose. The goods may be lent or hired
or deposited for safe custody or as security for a debt. The law contemplates delivery based upon a contract. Usually the delivery of goods
is the result of a contact. But this feature, though usual, is not essential. The supreme court has held that there can be bailment without a
contract.
(d) Obligation to Return the Goods or Dispose them according to directions of the Bailor- The essence of bailment is the obligation of the
bailee to return the goods or to dispose them according to the directions of the bailor. The directions for return or disposal of the goods
may be given even after the accomplishment of the purpose of bailment. Even where the contract is silent about the return of the goods,
there is an implied term in a bailment to return the goods within a reasonable time after the accomplishment of the purpose. It is not
bailment if there is no obligation to return the same subject matter either in its original or in altered form.
content.questionText:
G lived alone in a two storeyed building. He was to be sent on a business trip to Japan, from where he would not return before two
weeks. He asked H to take care of his house, as the crimes in the city had been on a rise. H readily agreed. G returned before the
stipulated time from his business trip, however H refused to vacate the house, and claimed that now he owns the house. Decide the case
as per the rules of breach of bailment contract.
options: This is not a breach of bailment contract because the house is an immovable property.
This is not a breach of bailment contract because G arrived before time.
This is a breach of bailment contract because G had entrusted H for care taking responsibility only.
This is a breach of bailment contract because H cannot become the owner of the property through a bailment contract.

to choose the most appropriate option which follows from the passage.


Passage – 4


A 'bailment' is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is
accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The person delivering the
goods is called the 'bailor'. The person to whom they are delivered is called the 'bailee'. The following are the essential features of
bailment:
(a) Specific Movable Property- A bailer-bailee relation can arise only in case of a specific movable property. There cannot be bailment of
immovable property.
(b) Delivery of Goods for Change of Possession- The essence of bailment is transfer of possession, ownership remaining with the bailor,
change of possession requires delivery of goods.
(c) Delivery for Some Purpose and Usually Upon a Contract- Delivery of goods should be for some purpose. The goods may be lent or hired
or deposited for safe custody or as security for a debt. The law contemplates delivery based upon a contract. Usually the delivery of goods
is the result of a contact. But this feature, though usual, is not essential. The supreme court has held that there can be bailment without a
contract.
(d) Obligation to Return the Goods or Dispose them according to directions of the Bailor- The essence of bailment is the obligation of the
bailee to return the goods or to dispose them according to the directions of the bailor. The directions for return or disposal of the goods
may be given even after the accomplishment of the purpose of bailment. Even where the contract is silent about the return of the goods,
there is an implied term in a bailment to return the goods within a reasonable time after the accomplishment of the purpose. It is not
bailment if there is no obligation to return the same subject matter either in its original or in altered form.

delivered in three days. The cake arrived in the morning, however T came to the shop in the evening to pick up the cake. When T checked
the cake, he saw that it was spoiled, which might be due to improper transportation or storage. T sued the bakery for breach of bailment,
however the bakery owner claimed that since T had already bought the cake, therefore no bailment contract arises. Decide the case.
